aardvark.context_blurb: The aardvark is a shy, nocturnal African mammal that lives in savannas and dry woodlands south of the Sahara. Its Afrikaans name means earth-pig, which fits: it has a long pig-like snout, a thick body, long rabbit-like ears, and strong digging claws that can carve a den out of hard red soil. DNA places the aardvark on its own branch of the mammal tree, distantly related to animals most people would never guess. It is a specialist, and almost every oddity in its body comes down to one job it does better than anything else in the bush.

aye-aye.context_blurb: The aye-aye is a nocturnal primate that lives only in the rainforests of Madagascar. It is a lemur, but it looks like no other primate on Earth: shaggy black fur, huge yellow eyes, giant leathery ears, and long bony fingers that end in curved claws. Many Malagasy villages have treated the aye-aye as a bad-luck omen for centuries, and it is now endangered. Scientists study it for the strange toolkit it uses to find a food source most other animals cannot reach at all.

babirusa.context_blurb: The babirusa is a wild pig that lives in the swampy rainforests of Sulawesi and nearby Indonesian islands. Males are famous for a bizarre set of tusks that curl in an unusual direction compared with any other pig. Babirusas are shy, mostly solitary, and quick runners for their size, and they wallow in mud and even swim between islands. The tusks and skull shape are what make scientists call this animal one of the strangest mammals alive.

binturong.context_blurb: The binturong, sometimes called a bearcat, is a shaggy, slow-moving mammal that lives in the tall rainforest canopies of Southeast Asia. It is neither a bear nor a cat; it belongs to a tropical group called viverrids and spends most of its life high in the trees, moving along branches on flat feet with a long muscular tail. Binturongs are mainly nocturnal, eat a lot of fruit, and are famous for a very particular smell that drifts off their fur and tells other binturongs they are nearby.

capybara.context_blurb: The capybara is the largest rodent in the world, a barrel-shaped grazing mammal of the wetlands, rivers, and flooded grasslands of South America. An adult can weigh as much as a grown person, yet it is calm and social, living in family groups that share water holes with caimans, herons, and even monkeys. Capybaras are built around a semi-aquatic life, and almost every feature of their bodies, from the position of their eyes to the webbing on their feet, is tuned for swimming and grazing at the water's edge.

fossa.context_blurb: The fossa is the top predator of Madagascar, a sleek, cat-like hunter that stalks lemurs through the island's rainforests and dry woodlands. It looks like a cross between a cougar and a mongoose, with a tail nearly as long as its body and semi-retractable claws for climbing. DNA shows the fossa is not a true cat at all; it belongs to a Madagascar-only family of carnivores descended from a single ancestor that drifted across from mainland Africa many millions of years ago.

giant-panda.context_blurb: The giant panda is a black-and-white bear that lives only in cool, misty mountain bamboo forests in central China. Although its gut is still built like a meat-eater's, almost every panda in the wild spends its day doing one thing: eating bamboo, for ten to sixteen hours at a stretch. Pandas are solitary, slow to breed, and a famous worldwide conservation symbol. Scientists study them for the many strange adaptations that let a bear survive on a plant that gives almost no calories.

kangaroo-rat.context_blurb: The kangaroo rat is a small, big-eyed desert rodent of the American Southwest and Mexico that bounds across hot sand on long back legs, like a tiny kangaroo. It is active only at night, lives in burrows it digs itself, and spends most of its life surrounded by seeds and dry heat. Its body is so finely tuned to the desert that it almost never drinks water. The way it manages to live its entire life without a sip is one of the most studied water tricks in all of mammal biology.

lowland-streaked-tenrec.context_blurb: The lowland streaked tenrec is a tiny Madagascar mammal that looks like a yellow-and-black striped hedgehog the size of a mouse. Tenrecs are not hedgehogs; they belong to an ancient Madagascar-only group of insect-eaters that have evolved to fill many niches on the island. The streaked tenrec is one of the few mammals in the world with a signaling trick scientists usually describe only in insects and snakes, which is why it keeps turning up in biology textbooks.

maned-wolf.context_blurb: The maned wolf is the tallest wild canid on Earth, a long-legged, fox-colored animal that walks the tall-grass savannas of central South America. Despite the name, it is not a true wolf or fox but the only living member of its genus. Maned wolves are solitary, mostly crepuscular, and known for a scent so sharp that people and zoo keepers can smell them long before they see one. Their diet is also unusual for a dog, leaning heavily on a single fruit of the savanna.

musk-ox.context_blurb: The musk ox is a shaggy, cold-adapted grazer of the Arctic tundra of Canada, Alaska, Greenland, and Siberia. It is not actually an ox; it is more closely related to sheep and goats, and it has survived from the ice age almost unchanged while mammoths and giant deer went extinct around it. Musk oxen live in small herds and have a famous group defense against wolves. Their skirts of fur, the longest of any land mammal, hide a second layer of wool so warm that people harvest it as one of the rarest fibers in the world.

numbat.context_blurb: The numbat is a small, striped marsupial that lives in a few patches of eucalyptus woodland in Western Australia. It is one of the rarest mammals on the continent, and unlike almost every other Australian marsupial it is active during the day, trotting across the forest floor with a bushy tail held high. Numbats are specialists on a single colonial insect, and almost every feature of their body, from the shape of their mouth to their peg-like teeth, is built around that one meal.

okapi.context_blurb: The okapi is a shy forest mammal that lives in the dense Ituri rainforest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its back half is striped like a zebra and its front half is a rich chocolate color, but DNA puts it in a family with only one other living member, which it does not look much like at all. Okapis were unknown to Western science until the early 1900s, which is extraordinary for a mammal this size. They are solitary, use scent trails to communicate, and have a very long dark tongue they use for grooming and feeding.

pink-fairy-armadillo.context_blurb: The pink fairy armadillo is the smallest armadillo in the world, a palm-sized burrower that lives in the dry sandy grasslands of central Argentina. Its shell is pink and only loosely attached to its back, which has puzzled naturalists ever since the species was first described in 1825. It spends almost its entire life underground, swimming through loose sand with huge front claws, and is so rarely seen above the surface that scientists still know very little about how it lives.

proboscis-monkey.context_blurb: The proboscis monkey is a leaf-eating primate that lives only in the mangrove and riverine forests of Borneo. Males are famous for a huge, floppy nose that keeps getting bigger as they age, while females have a much smaller upturned one. The monkeys live in troops along slow rivers, swim well, and have unusual digestive machinery for a primate because of a tough, leaf-heavy diet. The male's exaggerated feature turns out to be a signal that females notice, which is why it keeps growing.

quokka.context_blurb: The quokka is a small, cat-sized marsupial from a few islands and patches of mainland Western Australia, best known for a face that looks like it is permanently smiling. It is a nocturnal grazer that climbs small trees and shelters in dense scrub during the heat of the day. Quokkas have become famous worldwide for a tourist phenomenon on Rottnest Island, where the lack of ground predators has left them unusually tame around people.

red-panda.context_blurb: The red panda is a small, cat-sized mammal with a rust-red coat and a long striped tail that lives in the cool bamboo forests of the eastern Himalayas and southwestern China. Despite the name, it is not closely related to the giant panda; DNA places it on its own branch of the tree of life, the only living member of its family. Red pandas spend almost all their time in trees, feed mostly on bamboo, and are now classified as endangered because of habitat loss.

saiga-antelope.context_blurb: The saiga antelope is a goat-sized grazing mammal of the central Asian steppes, stretching across Kazakhstan, Russia, Mongolia, and Uzbekistan. It survived from the ice age, when it ranged all the way from Britain to Alaska, and is now critically endangered. The saiga is famous for a huge, drooping nose that looks almost like a short trunk and completely dominates its face. Scientists study the saiga partly for that strange nose and partly because the whole species has been hit by sudden mass die-offs.

slow-loris.context_blurb: The slow loris is a nocturnal primate that lives in the rainforests of South and Southeast Asia. It is about the size of a small cat, moves slowly along branches with a hand-over-hand grip, and has huge eyes for seeing in the dark. The slow loris has one trick that makes it unique among primates and is one of a handful of mammals in the world capable of what it does. Illegal pet-trade videos have made it famous online, which is a serious problem because these animals do not do well in captivity.

solenodon.context_blurb: The solenodon is a shrew-like mammal the size of a large rat that lives on Hispaniola and Cuba in the Caribbean. It is a living fossil: its lineage branched off from other mammals before the dinosaurs went extinct, and it has barely changed since. Solenodons have long rubbery snouts, grooved teeth, and a trick in common with only a tiny number of other mammals. Introduced predators have pushed them to the brink of extinction, and most people have never heard of them.

tarsier.context_blurb: The tarsier is a tiny nocturnal primate from the islands of Southeast Asia, including the Philippines and Indonesia. It fits in a human palm but has enormous golden eyes, each one bigger than its own brain, and long finger-pad hands for gripping bamboo. Tarsiers are strict meat-eaters, which is unusual for a primate, and they hunt insects, small lizards, and even bats by making stunning leaps in near-total darkness. Their eyes and ears are tuned to signals humans cannot share.

tasmanian-devil.context_blurb: The Tasmanian devil is a dog-sized carnivorous marsupial that lives only on the island of Tasmania. It is squat, black, and loud: devils are famous for ear-splitting screams at feeding scuffles, which is how European settlers gave them their name. They are scavengers as much as hunters, with a jaw pound-for-pound among the strongest of any mammal. In the past 30 years, a transmissible facial cancer has pushed the species toward collapse, and biologists are watching closely to see whether they can adapt.

antlion-the-larva-that-digs-a-sand-death.context_blurb: The antlion is a small, winged insect best known not as an adult but as its larva. The larva is a stubby, spiny creature that lives in dry, loose sand or dust in woodland corners and under overhangs on every continent except Antarctica. It is a sit-and-wait predator with a very specific hunting setup. Adult antlions look a bit like dragonflies but are only distantly related; the whole genius of the species is in the larval stage, which can last two or three years before the insect finally takes wing.

assassin-bug-the-ambush-hunter-that-wear.context_blurb: Assassin bugs are a huge family of long-legged, hook-beaked true bugs found all over the warm parts of the world. They are ambush predators that stalk other insects, stab them with a sharp proboscis, and suck them dry. Some species have developed a strange and gruesome trick to make themselves look even less like a predator while they hunt. Assassin bugs are also medically important because a few species in the Americas carry a human disease, but biologists keep coming back to them for their behavior.

atlas-moth-one-of-the-biggest-moths-with.context_blurb: The Atlas moth is one of the largest moths on Earth, with a wingspan up to about ten inches, and it lives in the tropical forests of South and Southeast Asia. The adult lives only a week or two, surviving on energy it stored as a caterpillar. The wingtips carry a famous pattern that scientists have argued about for a long time, because it looks uncannily like something else from the forest. Everything about the Atlas moth is scaled up to the limits of what an insect body can support.

bolas-spider-the-spider-that-fishes-with.context_blurb: The bolas spider is a small night-hunting spider found in the Americas, Africa, and Australasia. Unlike most spiders it does not build a flat web for catching prey; it specializes in catching one particular kind of insect using one very unusual tool. The hunting setup is so specific that the spider's chemistry and timing both have to line up with the behavior of its target. It is one of the clearest examples biologists have of a spider hunting more like a fisherman than a trap-weaver.

bullet-ant-the-worst-sting-on-the-schmid.context_blurb: The bullet ant is a large black ant that lives in the lowland rainforests of Central and South America. It nests at the base of trees and sends workers up into the canopy to forage. The ant is famous worldwide for its sting, which entomologists rank at the very top of a well-known pain scale. In parts of the Amazon the ant is also used in a Satere-Mawe coming-of-age ritual, and researchers come back to it over and over to study the chemistry of its venom.

diving-bell-spider-the-spider-that-lives.context_blurb: The diving bell spider is the only spider in the world that spends its entire adult life underwater. It lives in cool, slow ponds and weedy streams across Europe and parts of Asia. The spider hunts, mates, and raises its young beneath the surface, yet it still breathes air like any land spider; the puzzle of how it does that has fascinated naturalists since Victorian times. Its solution is elegant enough that engineers have borrowed the same name for a human diving device.

giant-weta-the-heavyweight-insect-of-new.context_blurb: The giant weta is a huge, flightless, cricket-like insect that lives only on a few small islands of New Zealand. Some of them are among the heaviest insects on Earth. Wetas are an ancient group, and they survived in New Zealand because the islands had no native land mammals, so they slowly took over the kinds of jobs mice and rats do in other ecosystems. They are now carefully protected, because introduced rats and stoats have pushed several species to the edge.

goliath-birdeater-the-biggest-spider-on-.context_blurb: The Goliath birdeater is the largest spider in the world by body mass, a dinner-plate-sized tarantula that lives in deep humid burrows of the Amazon rainforest in northern South America. Despite its name, it almost never eats birds; its usual prey are large insects, worms, and small frogs. The spider has urticating hairs on its abdomen that it flicks at threats, and it makes an audible hissing sound few other spiders can match. Biologists study it both for its size and for the limits of how big a spider can grow.

honeypot-ant-living-storage-jars-for-the.context_blurb: Honeypot ants are a group of ants that live in dry, hot places such as the deserts of Australia, Mexico, and the American Southwest. Food is rare and seasonal where they live, so the colony has evolved a strange and very specialized caste system in which some workers do almost nothing but store food on behalf of everyone else. These storage workers get so swollen they can barely move. Indigenous peoples of Australia have harvested honeypot ants as a traditional food for thousands of years.

jewel-wasp-the-wasp-that-turns-a-cockroa.context_blurb: The jewel wasp, also called the emerald cockroach wasp, is a brilliant metallic-green parasitoid wasp from tropical Africa, India, and the Pacific islands. It hunts cockroaches, and it does something to them that sounds like science fiction. The wasp uses the cockroach as a living nursery for its single offspring. Neuroscientists study its venom because it targets the roach's brain with surgical precision, blocking specific actions while leaving others intact in a way that is still not fully understood.

lord-howe-tree-lobster-the-stick-insect-.context_blurb: The Lord Howe tree lobster is a massive, dark-brown stick insect, big enough to fill a child's hand, that was thought extinct for more than 80 years after rats invaded its home island in the Pacific. Then biologists found a tiny population clinging to life in one specific place no rat could reach. The story of how it was rediscovered, bred in captivity, and prepared for release back to Lord Howe Island is one of the strangest comebacks in modern conservation.

new-zealand-glowworm-the-larva-that-fish.context_blurb: The New Zealand glowworm is not a worm at all but the larva of a small fly that lives inside damp caves and overhangs across New Zealand and parts of Australia. The larvae line cave ceilings with silk and hang long sticky threads below them, lit up by their own body chemistry. Tourists come from all over the world to see the ceilings covered in blue-green points of light. Scientists study the glowworm for both the chemistry of its light and the engineering of its silk.

ogre-faced-spider-the-net-caster-that-th.context_blurb: The ogre-faced spider, also called a net-casting spider, hunts at night in warm forests on several continents. Instead of waiting on a built web like most spiders, it holds a small, custom-made web stretched between its front legs and uses it as an active throwing net. It is named for a pair of enormous forward-facing eyes that give it one of the sharpest low-light visions of any arthropod. Scientists have recently shown that the spider can also detect prey without seeing them at all.

orchid-mantis-the-flower-that-eats-the-p.context_blurb: The orchid mantis is a small, pale pink or white praying mantis that lives in the rainforests of Southeast Asia. Its body is shaped and colored to look convincingly like a flower, down to petal-shaped flaps on its legs. For a long time naturalists assumed it was camouflaged for hiding, but careful fieldwork in the 2010s showed the whole setup is doing something more surprising than that, and biology textbooks have been rewriting the entry on it ever since.

tarantula-hawk-the-wasp-that-hunts-taran.context_blurb: The tarantula hawk is a very large, metallic-blue parasitoid wasp with rust-orange wings that is found in dry parts of the Americas, especially the American Southwest and Mexico. It hunts tarantulas, which are much bigger than it is, as food for its single offspring. The sting of a tarantula hawk is one of the most painful any insect can deliver, and the wasp has almost no natural predators because of it. Entomologists call it one of the clearest examples of an invertebrate specialist with no close rival.

trap-jaw-ant-jaws-that-snap-faster-than-.context_blurb: Trap-jaw ants are a group of ground-dwelling ants that live in warm forests around the world. Workers walk around with their mandibles cocked wide open like a mousetrap and then snap them shut on prey when sensory hairs are tripped. The speed of that snap puts the ant into the record books for one of the fastest motions ever measured in the animal kingdom. The ants also use the same mechanism in a surprising second way that has nothing to do with hunting.

treehopper-the-insect-with-alien-headgea.context_blurb: Treehoppers are small plant-sucking insects, related to cicadas, found in forests all over the world. They are famous among entomologists for a bizarre thing growing out of their backs: elaborate helmet-like shapes that can look like a thorn, an ant, a tiny mushroom, a wasp, or something out of a science-fiction comic. Scientists have argued for a century about how these helmets evolved and what they are really for. A single tropical forest can hold dozens of species, each with a different costume.

velvet-ant-the-cow-killer-that-is-really.context_blurb: The velvet ant, nicknamed the cow killer, is a brightly colored, fuzzy insect that walks across sunny ground in warm parts of North America. It is not actually an ant at all. The males have wings and look like typical wasps; the females are wingless and run across the ground, which is how the name got started. The velvet ant has one of the most painful stings of any insect in the United States, and it is also wrapped in several layers of defensive tricks on top of the sting.

velvet-worm-the-glue-cannon-hunter-of-th.context_blurb: Velvet worms are ancient, caterpillar-like animals that live in damp leaf litter in rainforests of the Southern Hemisphere, in places like South America, Australia, New Zealand, and southern Africa. They are not insects or worms; they are the only living members of their own branch of the tree of life, little changed from fossils more than 500 million years old. They are predators of small invertebrates, and they catch prey using a trick no other land animal has.

vinegaroon-the-whip-scorpion-that-sprays.context_blurb: The vinegaroon, also called a whip scorpion, is a nocturnal arachnid that lives in warm, dry regions from the American Southwest down into Mexico and parts of Asia. It looks like a scorpion crossed with a spider, with a long whip-like tail at the back instead of a stinger. Vinegaroons have no venom at all. Instead they defend themselves with a sharp-smelling chemical spray that scientists find useful partly because it comes out of the whip's base in a very precise, aimable jet.

zombie-ant-fungus-the-carpenter-ants-fat.context_blurb: The zombie-ant fungus is not actually an animal but a parasitic fungus of the genus Ophiocordyceps that infects carpenter ants in tropical rainforests, especially in Thailand and Brazil. The fungus takes over the ant's body in a very specific sequence of steps before killing it and bursting out to spread spores to the next victim. It is one of the most dramatic parasites known, and it has been featured in TV shows, video games, and medical research into fungal diseases.

armadillo-girdled-lizard-the-lizard-that.context_blurb: The armadillo girdled lizard is a small, armored lizard that lives in the rocky deserts of South Africa's western coast. Its body is covered in overlapping bony scales, and when threatened it folds up into a ring. The lizard is active during the day, feeds mainly on insects, and lives in small social groups in cracks between stones. Because of poaching for the pet trade, it is now a protected species, and its armor makes it one of the most-studied small reptiles in the dry-country lizard fauna of southern Africa.

basilisk-the-lizard-that-runs-on-water.context_blurb: The basilisk is a bright-green, long-tailed lizard that lives along forest streams and rivers in Central and South America. It is famous for an emergency escape trick it uses when a predator surprises it near water, which has given rise to a well-known nickname. The basilisk is omnivorous, lays its eggs on riverbanks, and can swim and dive underwater if the escape trick does not shake off the chase. Biologists study it as a textbook example of how an animal can briefly cheat the physics of its own weight.

caecilian-the-legless-amphibian-whose-yo.context_blurb: Caecilians are an entirely legless group of amphibians that burrow through warm, wet soil in the tropics of Africa, Asia, and the Americas. They look like big worms or small snakes but are more closely related to frogs than to any reptile. Caecilians are rarely seen above ground, feed on worms and small invertebrates, and have a tiny pair of sensory tentacles between their eyes and nostrils. The most unusual thing about them is a parenting trick a few species use that has forced biologists to redraw the standard chart of amphibian care.

darwins-frog-the-father-who-broods-young.context_blurb: Darwin's frog is a small, pointed-nosed frog that lives in the cool, mossy beech forests of southern Chile and Argentina. It was first described by Charles Darwin on his voyage of the Beagle in the 1830s and is now critically endangered. The frog is best known for an extraordinary parenting trick, in which the father does a job that in almost every other vertebrate is handled by the mother. Modern research is trying to figure out exactly how and when this strategy evolved.

draco-the-gliding-lizard-on-rib-wings.context_blurb: The Draco, also known as the flying dragon, is a small lizard that lives in the rainforest canopies of Southeast Asia and India. It spends most of its life clinging to tree trunks, where it is nearly invisible against the bark. When it needs to move between trees, it uses an anatomical trick that no other lizard has, flaring out a pair of wing-like flaps built from parts of its own skeleton. Draco cannot truly fly but can glide quite far between trunks without ever touching the ground.

flying-snake-the-serpent-that-glides.context_blurb: Flying snakes are a group of slender tree snakes that live in the forests of South and Southeast Asia. They do not have wings or any flap of extra skin, but they can glide long distances between trees anyway, steering with their bodies as they fall. Biologists at Virginia Tech have filmed them in slow motion to work out exactly how a snake with no limbs manages to turn gravity into a sideways jump. The snake is mildly venomous but harmless to humans; its real party trick is the glide.

gaboon-viper-the-longest-fangs-of-any-sn.context_blurb: The Gaboon viper is a thick, heavy snake that lives on the leaf-littered floors of African rainforests and woodlands. It is slow, patient, and almost invisible: the patterns on its back look exactly like dead leaves and dappled light. The Gaboon viper hunts by ambush and strikes with a weapon that puts it in a record book of its own among snakes. Despite its danger, it is a reclusive animal that rarely bites unless stepped on or handled.

hairy-frog-the-frog-that-breaks-its-own-.context_blurb: The hairy frog, also called the horror frog, is a stout frog from the rainforests of Central Africa. The nickname comes from thin skin filaments males grow during breeding season, which do a specific job tied to life in the fast streams where they live. The really strange thing about the hairy frog, though, is a defensive weapon it keeps hidden until a predator forces it out. Scientists first described the mechanism in the 1900s and have been studying it with X-rays and high-speed cameras ever since.

hellbender-the-giant-snot-otter-that-bre.context_blurb: The hellbender is a huge, flat-headed aquatic salamander that lives on the bottoms of cold, fast-flowing streams in the eastern United States. Adults can be nearly two feet long. The hellbender spends almost its entire life underwater, hiding beneath large flat rocks and ambushing crayfish, and it has a surprising answer to the problem of getting enough oxygen in cold water. The species is now in serious trouble because of pollution and the loss of the specific streambed shape it needs to lay eggs.

hognose-snake-the-drama-queen-death-fake.context_blurb: The eastern hognose snake is a stout, upturned-snout snake found across the eastern and central United States. It eats mostly toads and digs them out of sandy soil with its shovel-shaped nose. When threatened, the hognose puts on one of the most dramatic defensive shows of any animal in North America, moving through a whole sequence of bluffs before falling back on a last-ditch act. It is mildly venomous to its toad prey but harmless to humans; the real weapon is the performance.

leatherback-turtle-the-warm-blooded-rept.context_blurb: The leatherback sea turtle is the largest sea turtle on Earth, big enough that adults can weigh as much as a small car. Unlike other sea turtles, it has no hard shell: its back is a leathery hide stretched over a network of bony plates. Leatherbacks cross entire oceans between tropical nesting beaches and cold feeding grounds near the Arctic. They have a strange, mostly-jelly diet and a body-temperature strategy unusual for anything we normally call a reptile.

marine-iguana-the-only-sea-going-lizard.context_blurb: The marine iguana lives only on the Galapagos Islands and is the only lizard in the world that feeds in the sea. It is a stocky, dark-colored herbivore that dives into cold ocean water to graze on algae growing on submerged rocks. Marine iguanas are nothing like any mainland lizard; everything about them, from their snub-nosed heads to their flattened tails, has been reshaped by that one unusual meal. Charles Darwin, who famously called them imps of darkness, used them as evidence of how animals change over time.

mata-mata-turtle-the-leaf-that-vacuums-u.context_blurb: The mata mata is a strange, flat-headed turtle that lives on the leaf-covered bottom of slow-moving blackwater streams of the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Its shell is heavily ridged and its neck is covered in fringes and tabs of skin that break up its outline. The mata mata is almost completely motionless by day, waiting for fish to come close. When one does, it uses an eating method that lets it swallow prey without ever opening its mouth around them in the normal way.

olm-the-blind-cave-baby-dragon-that-live.context_blurb: The olm is a pale, finger-sized cave salamander that lives only in the limestone caves of southeastern Europe, mostly in Slovenia and the surrounding Dinaric Alps. Local people once gave it a legendary nickname after storms flushed washed-out olms out of caves. In complete darkness it never grows real adult eyes and never leaves its larval body. The olm has an extraordinarily slow metabolism, a very long lifespan for an amphibian, and a style of life that scientists keep studying for what it says about aging.

purple-frog-the-pig-nosed-frog-that-surf.context_blurb: The purple frog is a dark, bloated, pig-nosed frog that lives in the Western Ghats of India. It is one of the strangest frogs in the world, and it was only formally described by Western science in 2003. The frog spends almost its entire life hidden deep underground, feeding on termites, and surfaces for only a brief window each year to breed. Its evolutionary lineage splits off from almost every other living frog family and goes back to the age of the dinosaurs.

shingleback-skink-the-lizard-with-a-tail.context_blurb: The shingleback skink is a short, stocky Australian lizard with pine-cone-like scales. It is also called a sleepy lizard, bobtail, or stumpy. It lives in dry woodlands and grasslands across most of southern Australia and is usually seen basking on roadsides. The shingleback is unusual for a reptile in that it forms long-term monogamous pairs that return to each other every spring for many years. Its tail is also shaped and used in a specific way that fools a lot of predators.

spider-tailed-viper-the-tail-that-fishes.context_blurb: The spider-tailed horned viper is a small, dust-colored viper that lives in the rocky hills and ridges of western Iran. It is one of the most recently described venomous snakes, formally named in the 2000s, and biologists study it for a very specific hunting method it uses on migrating birds. The snake lies motionless among loose stones, waiting out the heat of the day, with only one tiny part of its body moving in a way that looks nothing like the rest of the snake at all.

surinam-toad-babies-that-erupt-from-the-.context_blurb: The Surinam toad is a flat, triangular, almost origami-shaped frog from the rivers and swamps of the Amazon basin. It is a lifelong swimmer and almost never leaves the water. Instead of a tongue, it uses sensitive fingertips to find prey in muddy water. The toad is best known among biologists for a reproductive strategy that is unlike anything else in the amphibian world and is the kind of thing people struggle to watch all the way through on video.

thorny-devil-drinking-through-skin-and-t.context_blurb: The thorny devil is a small, spiky lizard that lives in the dry deserts of central and western Australia. It is covered head to tail in sharp spines that make it look fierce, but the lizard is actually slow, harmless, and eats almost nothing except ants. The thorny devil's body is tuned around two very specific survival problems in the desert, and it has evolved separate, elegant solutions to each. Both solutions turn out to involve features that most people would never guess just from looking at it.

wallaces-flying-frog-the-frog-that-parac.context_blurb: Wallace's flying frog is a bright-green tree frog that lives in the rainforests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula. It was first described by the Victorian naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace during his years in the region in the 1850s. The frog spends almost all its time in the canopy, and when it needs to move between trees it does something no normal frog can do: it jumps and glides on a parachute built right into its own body.

why-the-ice-age-giants-died-overkill-vs-.context_blurb: At the end of the last ice age, between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most of the biggest land animals on every continent except Africa went extinct. Mammoths, giant sloths, saber-toothed cats, giant kangaroos, and many others disappeared in a wave that followed the arrival of modern humans and overlapped with sudden climate change. Scientists still argue about how much of the extinction was climate, how much was hunting pressure, and how much was both at once. The debate is one of the biggest in paleoecology.

archerfish.context_blurb: The archerfish is a small, striped tropical fish that lives in the mangrove swamps and brackish estuaries of Southeast Asia and northern Australia. It hunts in a way no other fish does, catching land insects without ever leaving the water. Juvenile archerfish practice the trick in groups until they are good at it; adults can be deadly accurate at surprising distances. Scientists study it both for how its eyes solve a tricky visual problem and for how its brain learns the physics involved.

box-jellyfish.context_blurb: The box jellyfish is a group of cube-shaped jellyfish that live in warm coastal waters, especially around northern Australia and the Indo-Pacific. They are pale, almost invisible in the water, and trail a cluster of long, thin tentacles beneath a boxy bell. Unlike most jellyfish they can swim actively, not just drift, and they have unusually sophisticated eyes for an animal with no central brain. Their sting is among the most dangerous of any animal on Earth.

coelacanth.context_blurb: The coelacanth is a huge, deep-dwelling lobe-finned fish that lives off the coasts of eastern Africa and Indonesia. For a long time scientists thought the whole group had gone extinct with the dinosaurs, until a live one turned up in a South African fishing net in 1938. It is one of the most famous living fossils, evolutionarily closer to lungfish and to the ancestors of all land vertebrates than it is to a tuna or a trout. Everything about its body carries clues to the deep history of our own skeleton.

cuttlefish.context_blurb: The cuttlefish is a short-bodied cephalopod related to octopuses and squid that lives in shallow seas around much of the world. It swims by rippling a long fin that runs down each side of its body. Cuttlefish are famous for their skin: in a fraction of a second they can turn themselves into a different pattern, texture, and color. They are also startlingly clever for an invertebrate, with large brains and complex visual tricks.

electric-eel.context_blurb: The electric eel is a long, dark fish of the slow, muddy rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Despite the name, it is not actually an eel but a kind of knifefish, more closely related to catfish. It is also one of only a handful of animals that can generate strong electric shocks, and it uses that electricity for many different jobs. Modern research has even shown it doing something no one expected a fish-shaped predator to do.

giant-and-colossal-squid.context_blurb: Giant and colossal squid are two different enormous deep-sea cephalopods that live far below the surface of the open ocean. Live sightings are extremely rare, and most of what scientists know about them comes from specimens recovered inside large predators that hunt them or washed up on remote beaches. Their eyes, their tentacles, and their life histories are all built for a world of near-total darkness and crushing pressure. The two species are not the same animal and have genuinely different body plans.

great-white-shark.context_blurb: The great white shark is a large, powerful shark that lives in cool and temperate oceans around the world, including the coasts of California, South Africa, Australia, and the Mediterranean. It can grow more than 20 feet long and is the biggest predatory fish alive today. Great whites hunt seals, sea lions, and other large marine prey using a mix of camouflage from below, bursts of speed, and senses tuned finely enough to pick up an injured animal at long range.

hammerhead-shark.context_blurb: The hammerhead shark is a group of shark species that live in warm oceans all over the world. They are named for the strange flattened, T-shaped extension of their heads, which is formally called a cephalofoil. The hammer is not a weapon in the usual sense; it is packed with sensors, and it changes how the shark hunts and swims. Some hammerhead species gather in enormous schools during the day in a few specific places, which is unusual for a predator this size.

horseshoe-crab.context_blurb: The horseshoe crab is a round, armored, almost helmet-shaped marine arthropod that lives in shallow water along the Atlantic coasts of North America and the Gulf and coasts of parts of Asia. It is not a true crab; it is more closely related to spiders and scorpions, and its lineage goes back more than 450 million years. Horseshoe crabs come ashore in huge spawning groups every spring. Modern medicine depends on them in a way most people never hear about.

mantis-shrimp.context_blurb: The mantis shrimp is a long, colorful marine crustacean that lives in warm shallow seas, mostly in burrows it digs in the sand. Despite the name, it is not a shrimp but belongs to its own ancient group called stomatopods. Mantis shrimp are famous for two things: a pair of hunting arms that strike with astonishing speed, and some of the most unusual eyes in the whole animal kingdom. Scientists keep updating what they think the shrimp can actually do with those eyes.

mudskipper.context_blurb: The mudskipper is a bulgy-eyed fish that lives in the tropical mudflats and mangrove swamps of Africa, Asia, and parts of Australia. Unlike almost every other fish, it spends most of its day out of the water. Mudskippers walk, climb, dig burrows, and even defend territories in the open air. They have adapted their eyes, gills, and skin to work both wet and dry, and they are one of the clearest living examples of how a fish body can be modified to spend time on land.

nautilus.context_blurb: The nautilus is a deep-sea cephalopod from the warm waters of the western Pacific. Unlike octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, it has kept the external shell that its ancestors wore for hundreds of millions of years. The shell is a beautiful coiled spiral divided into gas-filled chambers, which lets the nautilus float and sink without burning energy. Nautilus bodies also keep features that other cephalopods have lost, which is why biologists keep returning to it as a window into cephalopod history.

ocean-sunfish-mola.context_blurb: The ocean sunfish, also called the mola, is a huge, round, nearly tailless fish of the open ocean. Adults can weigh over a ton, which makes them the heaviest bony fish in the world. They drift on their sides at the surface, dive deep after jellyfish, and are often covered in parasites they clean off in a strange social arrangement with other animals. Despite their size, molas start life as microscopic larvae that are nothing like the adults, and the transformation between the two stages is one of the biggest size jumps in all of vertebrate biology.

octopus.context_blurb: The octopus is a soft-bodied cephalopod found in every ocean on Earth, from tide pools to the deep sea. It has eight arms covered in sensitive, grippy suckers, three hearts, and a nervous system split between a central brain and the arms themselves. Octopuses solve problems, open jars, remember individual humans, and change their skin in ways that make them one of the clearest cases of intelligence outside of vertebrates. Scientists study them to understand how a mind so different from ours can work at all.

pistol-shrimp.context_blurb: The pistol shrimp is a small marine crustacean that lives in warm, shallow seas around the world. It has one normal pincer and one enormous one, and it uses the big one as a weapon in a way that would be hard to believe without high-speed video. Pistol shrimp also share burrows with gobies in one of the ocean's clearest examples of two unrelated species living together to each other's benefit.

portuguese-man-o-war.context_blurb: The Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish but is actually something much stranger: an entire colony of specialized animals that live and work together as one unit. It drifts on the surface of warm ocean currents, especially the Atlantic and Pacific trade-wind zones, under a glassy, blue-tinted gas-filled float. Beneath the float trail long stinging tentacles that paralyze fish. The sting is painful to humans but almost never fatal; the man o' war's real trick is a kind of cooperation most animals cannot pull off.

sea-cucumber.context_blurb: The sea cucumber is a sausage-shaped marine invertebrate that lives on the sea floor in every ocean, from shallow reefs down into the deep abyss. Despite its soft, slow look, it is an echinoderm, a cousin of sea stars and sea urchins. The sea cucumber feeds by vacuuming up sand or filtering water, and when threatened it has a bizarre and genuinely weird defensive move that most people, on seeing it the first time, have trouble believing is real.

sea-star.context_blurb: The sea star, sometimes called the starfish, is a radially symmetric marine animal that lives in oceans worldwide, from shallow tide pools to the deep sea. It is not a fish at all; it is an echinoderm, a cousin of sea urchins, sand dollars, and sea cucumbers. Sea stars have no brain and no blood in the usual sense. They move, feed, and heal using a surprising hydraulic system under their skin and a few other tricks that biologists have been peeling apart for over a hundred years.

seahorse.context_blurb: The seahorse is a small, upright-swimming fish that lives in shallow, warm, seagrass-filled waters around much of the world. It has a horse-shaped head, a prehensile tail that grips weeds like a monkey's, and a cluster of body-plan features that make it one of the strangest fish on Earth. Everything about the seahorse is slow and precise, from how it feeds to how it reproduces. The male and female of a pair tend to stay together for a long time.

whale-shark.context_blurb: The whale shark is the biggest fish in the ocean, a slow, spotted shark that can grow more than 40 feet long. It lives in warm seas around the world and is a specialist on some of the smallest food in the sea. Whale sharks gather in a few predictable places each year, which is where researchers and tourists go to see them. The entire body of this huge animal is built around that one specialized meal, and biologists are still learning where they go when they leave the known gathering sites.

beaver.context_blurb: The beaver is a large, semi-aquatic rodent that lives along streams and rivers across North America and Eurasia. It is one of the only animals that reshapes the shape of its own habitat on a large scale, turning streams into ponds and ponds into wet meadows. Beavers are expert swimmers with waterproof fur, a flat scaly tail, and some of the most unusual teeth in any mammal. Modern conservation uses them as ecosystem engineers to restore degraded landscapes.

camel.context_blurb: The camel is a large, long-legged mammal that lives in the deserts of North Africa, the Middle East, and Central Asia, with a close cousin in the cold deserts of Mongolia. People have used camels for thousands of years as pack animals, mounts, and sources of milk and wool, but a camel's biology is interesting on its own. The animal's body is built around one hard problem of desert life, and the solution shows up in almost every part of it, from blood cells shaped unlike any other mammal's to kidneys that squeeze water out of urine in a very particular way.

cheetah.context_blurb: The cheetah is a slender, long-legged cat that lives on the savannas and dry grasslands of Africa, with a tiny last population in Iran. It is the fastest land animal on Earth, built around sprinting rather than wrestling or climbing. Cheetahs are also unusual among big cats for their social lives: females live alone with their cubs, but brothers often form hunting coalitions that last for life. The species faces a specific long-term problem that has become one of the central puzzles of modern cheetah conservation.

echidna.context_blurb: The echidna is a short, spiny mammal that lives in Australia and New Guinea. Along with the platypus, it is one of the only two living kinds of mammal that still lays eggs, a trait kept from a lineage older than the dinosaurs. Echidnas live mostly solitary lives, dig for ants and termites, and have a snout packed with sensors that would be impressive on any animal. They also do some things related to reproduction and temperature control that remind biologists how strange their family tree is.

elephant.context_blurb: The elephant is the largest land animal on Earth. There are three living species: the African savanna, the African forest, and the Asian elephant. All three live in close family groups led by an older female, and all three have the same long, muscular, boneless trunk, which is one of the most capable grasping organs in the animal kingdom. Elephants are famously intelligent and emotionally complex. Biologists study them for their communication, their memory, and their long slow life histories.

giraffe.context_blurb: The giraffe is the tallest living land animal, a long-legged, long-necked ruminant of the savannas and woodlands of Africa. Adults can be nearly 18 feet tall. Giraffes feed in the tops of acacia trees, live in loose herds with no permanent leader, and have a prehensile tongue they use to pluck leaves around thorns. Their heart, blood pressure, legs, and neck are all engineered for the problem of being that tall, and they do several things related to that problem no other mammal does.

gray-wolf.context_blurb: The gray wolf is the biggest living wild dog, native to forests, tundras, and mountains across the northern hemisphere. Wolves live in close-knit family packs, hunt large prey cooperatively, and range over huge territories that they defend with scent marks and howling. Dogs, domesticated long ago, descend from wolves, which is why so many of the things dogs do have wolf origins. Modern wolf biology has become one of the clearest stories in ecology about how a top predator shapes an ecosystem.

hippopotamus.context_blurb: The hippopotamus is a huge, barrel-shaped mammal of rivers and shallow lakes across sub-Saharan Africa. Despite the name, which means river horse, hippos are not related to horses at all; their closest living relatives are whales and dolphins, and the two groups share a surprising number of body-plan features underneath. Hippos spend their days in the water and come out at night to graze, and they are, pound for pound, one of the most dangerous large mammals to humans on the continent.

honey-badger.context_blurb: The honey badger is a stocky, low-slung carnivore that lives across much of Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. It is only distantly related to true badgers; it is more like an oversized weasel. The honey badger has a reputation as one of the toughest small predators on Earth. It will take on cobras, porcupines, and even young lions, and it tends to win in ways that have made it a favorite animal of wildlife documentaries. Its skin and chemistry help explain how it gets away with it.

kangaroo.context_blurb: The kangaroo is a group of large marsupials that live in Australia, where they are the dominant native grazer. The biggest, the red kangaroo, can top six feet standing up. Kangaroos travel using one of the most efficient movement systems any big animal has ever evolved, and they also do things related to reproduction and group life that no placental mammal matches. They are now so numerous in parts of the Australian outback that they are managed as both an icon and a problem.

koala.context_blurb: The koala is a small, grey, pouched tree-climbing marsupial that lives in the eucalyptus forests of eastern Australia. It is one of the pickiest eaters in the mammal world, surviving almost entirely on a single kind of plant that is tough, oily, and mildly poisonous. Koalas spend most of the day asleep because that diet gives so little energy. The animal is a specialist in every sense, from its gut to its paws to the slow rhythm of its day, and it is now listed as endangered in some Australian states after years of habitat loss and fire.

naked-mole-rat.context_blurb: The naked mole-rat is a small, pink, nearly hairless rodent that lives in long underground tunnels in the dry grasslands of East Africa. It looks almost like a wrinkled little sausage with teeth. The naked mole-rat is extraordinary among mammals for its social life, which is organized more like a bee colony than like a rodent nest. It is also extraordinary for how long it lives, how little it ages, and how it handles conditions that would kill almost any other mammal. Biomedical researchers study it closely for exactly these reasons.

pangolin.context_blurb: The pangolin is a scale-covered mammal that lives in Africa and across much of South and Southeast Asia. It is sometimes called a scaly anteater, but it is not closely related to anteaters at all; it belongs to its own order of mammals. Pangolins eat almost nothing except ants and termites, which they lap up with a tongue that is extraordinary even by the standards of ant-eaters. They are now the most trafficked mammal in the world because of demand for their scales, and every living species is at serious risk.

platypus.context_blurb: The platypus is a small, duck-billed, beaver-tailed mammal that lives in the freshwater streams and rivers of eastern Australia. When the first platypus specimen reached European naturalists in 1799, many assumed it was a fake. The platypus is a monotreme, one of only two mammal groups still laying eggs, and it has an unusually long list of features that no other living mammal shares. It swims with its eyes shut, finds prey with senses other mammals do not have, and the males carry a weapon unique among furred animals.

polar-bear.context_blurb: The polar bear is a huge white bear that lives on the sea ice of the Arctic, from northern Canada and Alaska through Greenland and the Russian coast. Polar bears are the most carnivorous of all bears, specializing in seals they hunt from the edges of ice floes. Their fur, their fat, and even the skin under their fur are all tuned to the problem of staying warm in cold water and cold wind. Climate change is now reshaping their habitat faster than almost any other large mammal has to deal with.

sloth.context_blurb: The sloth is a group of slow-moving, long-clawed mammals that live upside down in the rainforest canopies of Central and South America. There are two living families, three-toed and two-toed, and both move more slowly than almost any other mammal. Sloths descend to the ground only every week or so and do almost everything, including eat, sleep, and give birth, hanging from branches. Their slowness is a strategy, not an accident, and it drives several surprising ecological relationships.

star-nosed-mole.context_blurb: The star-nosed mole is a small, nearly blind, insect-eating mammal that lives in the wet soils and shallow ponds of the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. The animal is best known for the strange, 22-fingered pink rosette on the tip of its snout. The star is not an olfactory organ; it is a touch organ, and it operates at a speed that puts the star-nosed mole into the record books among mammals. Scientists study it closely for what it says about how brains handle rapid sensory information.

vampire-bat.context_blurb: The vampire bat is a small bat that feeds entirely on the blood of other animals. There are three living species, all in Central and South America. The vampire bat is extraordinary in several ways: it can run on the ground almost like a four-legged animal, it shares food with roost-mates that are starving, and it has a specific set of body features for its very specialized meal. Scientists have also learned surprising things from vampire bats about how memory, friendship, and reciprocity work in a non-primate brain.

wolverine.context_blurb: The wolverine is a stocky, bear-like mammal that lives in the boreal forests and mountain tundras of the far north, across Scandinavia, Russia, Canada, and Alaska. It is one of the most powerful carnivores for its size on Earth and can drive even wolves and bears off a kill. Wolverines range over huge territories, cache food in the snow for lean times, and are built around life in deep cold. They are rare, hard to find, and remain one of the least-studied large carnivores in North America.

barreleye-macropinna-microstoma.context_blurb: The barreleye is a small deep-sea fish that lives several hundred meters down in the open ocean, most famously off California and Hawaii. For decades it was known only from damaged specimens hauled up in trawl nets. In 2009, underwater video from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute finally showed a live barreleye, and the footage revealed something about its head that no one had seen before. The fish is a slow, hovering predator that lives in the perpetual twilight zone and solves one specific hunting problem in a very unusual way.

blobfish-psychrolutes-marcidus.context_blurb: The blobfish is a soft, flabby deep-sea fish that lives on the bottom off the coasts of Australia, Tasmania, and New Zealand. It became internet-famous for a photograph taken on the deck of a trawler, which shows a sad, melted-looking face. The photograph is a very poor representation of what the fish looks like in its real home. Everything about the blobfish's body is a solution to the pressures and temperatures of the deep seabed, and the famous droopy face is a side effect of pulling the animal out of that world.

deep-sea-anglerfish-ceratioidei.context_blurb: The deep-sea anglerfish is a group of several hundred species that live in the dark middle and lower layers of the world's oceans, far below the surface. The females are large, ugly ambush predators with a glowing lure that dangles over their mouths. The males are tiny by comparison and lead a very different kind of life. Reproduction in deep-sea anglerfish is one of the strangest arrangements in the vertebrate world and has been giving biology textbooks a reliable showpiece for over a century.

electric-catfish-malapteruridae.context_blurb: The electric catfish is a family of large freshwater catfish that live in slow, muddy rivers across much of tropical Africa, including the Nile. They are strong, nocturnal predators with soft, scaleless skin. Electric catfish are one of only a handful of fish groups that generate their own strong electrical shocks, and the people of ancient Egypt knew them long before any modern biologist did. Modern research is still mapping out exactly how the catfish's body produces and controls those shocks.

elephantnose-fish-gnathonemus-petersii.context_blurb: The elephantnose fish is a small, dark freshwater fish from the muddy, slow rivers of West and Central Africa. The name comes from a long, finger-like projection on its lower jaw, which it uses to probe the river bottom for food. Elephantnose fish are nocturnal and hunt in near-total darkness, and they have one of the largest brains for their body size of any fish on Earth. Most of that brain is wired to one particular sensory system that lets them map the world without seeing it.

flashlight-fish-anomalopidae.context_blurb: The flashlight fish is a small, dark reef fish that lives in warm tropical oceans around the world and is best known in the Caribbean, the Indo-Pacific, and the Red Sea. The fish spends the day in deep water or inside caves and comes out at night to feed. It is named for a pair of large patches of glowing tissue on its face, which it can switch on and off like a car headlight. The light does several jobs for the fish, and researchers have carefully worked out what each of them is.

frogfish-antennariidae.context_blurb: The frogfish is a small, lumpy, almost spherical fish that lives on tropical and subtropical reefs around the world. It is one of the ocean's great disguise artists, so well matched to sponges, corals, and seaweed that divers can swim right past one without seeing it. Frogfish are ambush hunters, and they walk across the bottom on modified fins rather than really swimming. They also use a built-in lure in a way that is more carefully controlled than most people would expect from a fish.

gulper-eel-pelican-eel-eurypharynx-pelec.context_blurb: The gulper eel, also called the pelican eel, is a slender deep-sea fish that lives at depths of about one to two miles down in the open ocean. It has a tiny head, a huge expandable mouth, a stretchy stomach, and a long whip-like tail. Live gulper eels are almost never seen; most specimens come from trawl nets. In 2018, a video from a submersible caught one doing something unexpected, which quickly went viral in scientific circles.

handfish-brachionichthyidae.context_blurb: Handfish are a group of extremely rare, hand-sized fish that live only in a few patches of sea bottom around Tasmania. Instead of swimming, they walk across the sand on fins that look remarkably like little hands. There are several species, and some are among the most endangered fish in the world. Everything about the handfish, from its movement to its tiny range to its unusual eggs, is of close interest to Australian marine biologists.

hatchetfish-sternoptychidae.context_blurb: The hatchetfish is a small, flat-sided deep-sea fish shaped like the blade of a hatchet. It lives in the upper mesopelagic zone, several hundred meters down in oceans around the world. Hatchetfish are silvery, mirror-sided fish with huge upward-facing eyes and a line of light-producing organs along their undersides. That light is used in a specific survival trick that is one of the clearest examples of how a fish can hide in open water that has nowhere to hide at all.

leafy-sea-dragon-phycodurus-eques.context_blurb: The leafy sea dragon is a close relative of the seahorse that lives only off the southern coast of Australia. It is covered in long, leaf-shaped flaps of skin that blend in perfectly with the swaying kelp forests where it lives. The sea dragon is a slow, drifting predator on tiny crustaceans, and it does not swim with any of the usual power. Breeding sea dragons also share some of the strange reproductive habits of their seahorse cousins.

oarfish-regalecus-glesne.context_blurb: The oarfish is a long, silvery, ribbon-shaped fish that lives in the open ocean a few hundred meters below the surface. It can grow more than 20 feet long, which may make it the longest bony fish in the world. Oarfish are almost never seen alive; most known specimens are animals that washed up on beaches or came up sick. Their shape, size, and bright-red fins have fueled a very long history of sea-serpent stories around the world.

sarcastic-fringehead-neoclinus-blanchard.context_blurb: The sarcastic fringehead is a small, bad-tempered fish of the shallow coastal waters off California and Baja California. It is a territorial ambush hunter that lives inside empty shells, bottles, and crevices on the sea floor. The fringehead is best known among divers for an aggressive display it uses against rivals, which involves part of its own anatomy doing something no fish would be expected to do. Its face has gone viral in underwater photography more than once.

sheepshead-fish-archosargus-probatocepha.context_blurb: The sheepshead is a striped, panfish-sized fish of the shallow Atlantic coast of North America, from New York down into the Gulf of Mexico. It is a popular target for anglers in Florida and the Carolinas. The sheepshead lives mostly around rocks, pilings, and oyster beds, and it has an unusual set of teeth for a fish, teeth that look so much like a human mouth that photos of them regularly surprise people on the internet.

snakehead-fish-channidae.context_blurb: The snakehead fish is a family of long, air-breathing predatory fish native to Africa and Asia. They are famous among biologists both for their aggressive hunting behavior in their native rivers and for the environmental damage they can cause when released into waterways where they do not belong. Snakeheads have a trick in their respiratory system that lets them survive out of water for far longer than most fish could ever manage, and they can even cross small stretches of land between pools.

stargazer-uranoscopidae.context_blurb: The stargazer is a group of thickset, bottom-living fish that live buried in sand on continental shelves around the world. They are ambush predators, with eyes and mouths pointed straight up, so that they lie almost flat under the sand and strike at whatever swims directly over them. Stargazers combine several defensive and offensive tricks that very few other fish put together on the same body, including features that make them dangerous to step on.

stonefish-synanceia.context_blurb: The stonefish is a small, lumpy, ugly fish that lives on tropical reefs and rocky shallows across the Indo-Pacific. It is the most venomous fish in the world. Stonefish spend their days half-buried in sand or wedged among coral rubble, where they are nearly invisible. Everything about them, from the texture of their skin to their defensive spines, is a precise solution to the problem of being a slow, chunky fish on a reef full of fast ones.

viperfish-chauliodus.context_blurb: The viperfish is a small, nightmare-looking deep-sea predator that lives several hundred meters down in warm and temperate oceans around the world. It has a long, fang-filled jaw, a glowing lure near its back, and a body that often looks almost transparent. The viperfish is one of the clearest examples of how a predator in the dark middle layers of the ocean has to combine stealth, lure, and strike to make a living on scarce prey.

blanket-octopus-tremoctopus.context_blurb: The blanket octopus is an octopus of the open ocean, drifting through warm tropical and subtropical seas around the world. The females are large, up to about two meters, and trail long sheets of webbing between their arms when they open up, which is where the name comes from. The males are a tiny fraction of the size of the females, which is already one of the strangest differences in the animal kingdom. The blanket octopus also has a defensive and offensive trick that no other octopus is known to use.

blue-dragon-nudibranch-glaucus-atlanticu.context_blurb: The blue dragon is a tiny, electric-blue sea slug that drifts at the surface of warm oceans around the world. It is only about an inch long. The blue dragon feeds on dangerous jellyfish and jelly-like animals, including the Portuguese man o' war, and it is tough enough to collect what should be a deadly chemical from them and reuse it as its own weapon. Everything about the little slug, from its color to the way it floats, is tuned to a very hard life at the open-ocean surface.

blue-ringed-octopus-hapalochlaena.context_blurb: The blue-ringed octopus is a very small octopus that lives in tide pools and shallow reefs across the Indo-Pacific, especially around Australia, Japan, and the Philippines. It is one of the most venomous animals in the sea, despite being easy to miss if you are not looking for it. When threatened, it lights up with brilliant blue rings that pulse against a yellow background, giving a warning that most predators learn to respect. Its venom and nervous system behavior are both tightly studied by medical researchers.

bobbit-worm-eunice-aphroditois.context_blurb: The bobbit worm is a long, iridescent marine worm that lives buried in the sand of tropical reefs around the world, with only its head sticking out. The worm can grow more than two meters long, with hooked jaws that snap shut on anything that swims close enough. Divers see them most often around warm Pacific reefs, where the worms strike so fast on video they look like a trap being sprung. The bobbit worm is one of the clearest examples of a sit-and-wait ocean predator built around pure ambush.

christmas-tree-worm-spirobranchus-gigant.context_blurb: The Christmas tree worm is a small marine worm that lives permanently inside tubes it bores into coral heads on tropical reefs around the world. The only part of the worm most divers ever see is a pair of spiral, many-colored crowns that look like tiny Christmas trees. The crowns handle feeding and breathing at the same time. When anything touches them, they vanish into the coral in a blink in one of the fastest withdrawal reflexes any invertebrate has.

coconut-crab-birgus-latro.context_blurb: The coconut crab is a huge terrestrial hermit crab that lives on tropical islands across the Indian and western Pacific Oceans. Adults can span three feet from leg to leg and weigh several kilograms, and unlike other hermit crabs, they drop their borrowed shell as they grow and harden their own back instead. Their claws are strong enough to crack open the fruit the species is named for, and biologists have measured their grip strength and found it is near the top of the invertebrate world.

comb-jelly-ctenophora.context_blurb: The comb jelly is a group of transparent, soap-bubble-shaped marine animals found in oceans everywhere, from coastal bays to the deep sea. They are not jellyfish; they are their own ancient branch of the tree of life, and some scientists think they are the oldest surviving animal lineage. Comb jellies swim by beating rows of tiny hair-like plates that run down their bodies, which refract light into shimmering rainbow waves. The animal has no stinging cells and no central brain, yet it hunts actively and in some cases traps prey in sticky cells unique to its group.

dumbo-octopus-grimpoteuthis.context_blurb: The Dumbo octopus is a soft, pale, deep-sea octopus that lives on the sea floor at depths from a few hundred to several thousand meters, in every ocean of the world. It is named for a pair of flaps on top of its mantle that it flaps slowly to swim, which reminded zoologists of the Disney elephant. The Dumbo octopus is much less aggressive than its shallow-water cousins and lives in a cold, dark environment where food is sparse. Everything about it is tuned to that slow, hushed world.

flamboyant-cuttlefish-metasepia-pfefferi.context_blurb: The flamboyant cuttlefish is a small cuttlefish that lives on sandy or muddy seabeds across the tropical Indo-Pacific, from Indonesia to northern Australia. It is only a few inches long, but it is one of the brightest cephalopods on Earth: when disturbed, its skin ripples with a hypnotic display of magenta, yellow, and white. The flamboyant cuttlefish also walks on the sand rather than swims, and the chemistry behind its appearance has its own research literature.

giant-isopod-bathynomus-giganteus.context_blurb: The giant isopod is a deep-sea crustacean that looks like a huge, pale cousin of the common pill bug. It lives on the cold seafloor of the Atlantic and Pacific down to about 2,000 meters. Giant isopods are scavengers, feeding on the sinking bodies of larger animals, and they can go for astonishingly long periods between meals without dying. A famous research aquarium in Japan kept one alive without feeding it for years, which is why the giant isopod has become something of an internet celebrity.

giant-tube-worm-riftia-pachyptila.context_blurb: The giant tube worm is a huge red-tipped worm that lives in dense clusters on the deep ocean floor, especially along the East Pacific Rise. The animal has no mouth, no gut, and no anus. It feeds instead by growing a huge internal community of bacteria inside its own body and sharing chemicals with them in a trade neither partner can run alone. The giant tube worm overturned a huge amount of what biologists thought about where life can live when it was discovered in 1977.

sea-angel-clione.context_blurb: The sea angel is a tiny, transparent sea slug that lives in cold ocean waters, especially around the Arctic and Antarctic. It swims by flapping two wing-like fins that make it look like a floating cherub. Sea angels are predators, and they feed almost exclusively on one specific prey item that they hunt with a surprising piece of equipment. For something that drifts through dark polar seas and looks delicate enough to break, the sea angel is actually a very committed hunter.

vampire-squid-vampyroteuthis-infernalis.context_blurb: The vampire squid is a small, dark, deep-sea cephalopod of the oxygen-minimum layer in warm oceans around the world. Despite its name, it is not a true squid or an octopus; it is the only living member of its own order, with a mix of features from both groups. The vampire squid has webbing between its arms, light-producing patches scattered over its body, and a defensive behavior that makes dramatic use of the webbing. Its diet turned out to be nothing like what people assumed from its name.

venuss-flower-basket-euplectella-aspergi.context_blurb: Venus's flower basket is a deep-sea sponge that lives on the sea floor of the western Pacific. The animal is a hollow, cylindrical cage made of fused glass fibers, and in the dim light of the deep ocean it looks like a woven lantern. The sponge is famous for a specific relationship it has with a pair of shrimp that live trapped inside it for life. The structural engineering of the sponge's glass skeleton is also carefully studied for what it says about building strong materials from brittle parts.

yeti-crab-kiwa.context_blurb: The yeti crab is a group of pale, blind deep-sea crustaceans discovered in 2005 on the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge. The crabs live around hot hydrothermal vents a mile or more below the surface, and their most striking feature is a thick layer of hair-like bristles covering their claws and legs. Those bristles are not just decoration; the yeti crab grows a crop of chemosynthetic bacteria in them that it uses in a very specific way. The animal is one of the clearest living examples of ocean life running on the chemistry of the vents, not sunlight.

club-winged-manakin.context_blurb: The club-winged manakin is a small, brightly colored forest bird that lives in the cloud forests of western Colombia and Ecuador. Males gather on display branches to attract females, and the show they put on involves sound rather than dance. The club-winged manakin is one of only two birds in the world known to make a certain kind of music, and the way its body produces that sound required scientists to rewrite part of what they thought was possible for a bird's anatomy.

frogmouth.context_blurb: The frogmouth is a group of nocturnal birds that live in Australia and Southeast Asia. By day, they sit motionless on branches with their beaks pointed upward, blending into the bark so completely that most people will walk right past one without seeing it. Despite the owl-like look and nighttime habits, frogmouths are not owls. They have a huge, frog-shaped mouth they open very wide to catch insects and small prey, and the way they hunt is unlike almost any other bird of their size.

harpy-eagle.context_blurb: The harpy eagle is a huge, powerful eagle that lives in the rainforests of Central and South America. It is one of the largest eagles in the world and the top aerial predator of the Amazon canopy. Harpies hunt from perches rather than from soaring flight, and their talons are built for a very specific kind of prey. The bird is now threatened across much of its range because of deforestation, and conservation projects in Panama and Brazil are trying to protect what is left.

hoatzin.context_blurb: The hoatzin is a strange, pheasant-sized bird that lives in flooded forests along the Amazon and Orinoco rivers of South America. It has a spiky punk-rock crest, a blue face, and a shuffling, clumsy way of moving through the trees. The hoatzin eats almost nothing but leaves, which is almost unheard-of among flying birds, and its gut is more like a cow's than a sparrow's. Its chicks also carry a feature almost no other living bird has.

hoopoe.context_blurb: The hoopoe is a slender, cinnamon-colored bird with a long curved bill and a dramatic black-and-white crest. It lives across Europe, Africa, and much of Asia and spends most of its time on the ground, probing for insects. The hoopoe has turned up in art, poetry, and religious writing from ancient Egypt to the Qur'an, and it is the national bird of Israel. Nesting hoopoes also combine several defensive tricks that have been giving ornithologists material to study for a long time.

kakapo.context_blurb: The kakapo is a huge, flightless, nocturnal parrot that lives only on a few predator-free islands off the coast of New Zealand. There are only about 250 individuals left, each one of them named by biologists. The kakapo is unlike any other parrot: it is heavier than any other, cannot fly, lives on the ground, and breeds only every few years, when a specific food source is abundant. The whole species is one of the most closely managed in the world.

kea.context_blurb: The kea is a large, olive-green parrot that lives only in the mountains of New Zealand's South Island. Keas live where snow sits for much of the year, and they get through that life with a combination of curiosity, playfulness, and problem-solving that puts them in the same mental league as crows and apes. They are also notorious for a specific habit at mountain parking lots that keeps them in the news.

marabou-stork.context_blurb: The marabou stork is a huge, bald-headed scavenging bird that lives across sub-Saharan Africa. It has one of the largest wingspans of any living bird and often weighs more than a human child. The marabou's bare head, huge beak, and dangling throat pouch are the kinds of features that get written into Victorian descriptions as hideous, but each of them is doing a specific job tied to how the bird feeds. Marabou storks are important parts of the African scavenger community.

oilbird.context_blurb: The oilbird is a nocturnal fruit-eating bird that lives in caves in the forested parts of northern South America and Trinidad. It is the only bird in the world that both lives in a cave in deep darkness and also eats only fruit. The oilbird uses a specialized sense to navigate through pitch-black cave passages, which is otherwise mostly associated with bats. Humans once hunted oilbirds for the thick layer of fat on their chicks, which gave the bird its name.

potoo.context_blurb: The potoo is a group of large, nocturnal birds that live in the forests of Central and South America. By day, a potoo sits on a broken-off branch stump with its beak pointed upward and its eyes mostly closed, blending into the stump so perfectly that it looks like part of the tree. At night, it hunts flying insects by diving from its perch and sailing back. The way the potoo spends its day is one of the most reliable camouflage tricks any bird has.

secretarybird.context_blurb: The secretarybird is a tall, long-legged bird of prey that walks across the savannas and grasslands of sub-Saharan Africa. It is unmistakable in silhouette, with the body of an eagle on the legs of a stork. The secretarybird can fly, but it does most of its hunting on foot. Its signature method of killing prey is unusual among raptors and gives it one of the strangest fight styles in the bird world. It is now listed as endangered as its grassland habitat shrinks.

superb-bird-of-paradise.context_blurb: The superb bird-of-paradise is a small, jet-black forest bird that lives in the rainforests of New Guinea. Males put on one of the most carefully choreographed courtship displays in the whole bird world, transforming themselves into a shape and face that look nothing like a normal bird. For a long time the superb bird-of-paradise was treated as one species. Modern DNA work has split it into at least two, each with slightly different dance moves.

sword-billed-hummingbird.context_blurb: The sword-billed hummingbird is a hummingbird that lives in the Andean cloud forests of northern South America. It is the only bird in the world with a bill of its particular shape and proportions. The sword bill is tied closely to a specific set of flowers it feeds from and to a problem of coevolution that keeps turning up in ecology textbooks. The way the bird grooms, perches, and sleeps all has to be adapted around that oversized bill.

toucan.context_blurb: The toucan is a group of brightly colored forest birds that live in the warm rainforests of Central and South America. They are famous for huge, cartoonish bills that are often as long as the rest of their body. The bill looks heavy but is a lightweight sponge-like structure inside, and biologists have shown that it does more than one job for the bird at the same time. Toucans are also surprisingly social for a bird of their size and are often seen in loose flocks moving through the canopy.

vulture.context_blurb: Vultures are a group of large scavenging birds that live on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They clean up carcasses that would otherwise rot and spread disease, and the ecosystem job they do is far bigger than most people realize until it stops. Vultures are extremely well equipped for a diet of dead flesh, with chemistry and anatomy tuned to a job no other large bird will take. Several vulture populations around the world have collapsed in the last few decades, and the knock-on effects have been severe.

albatross.context_blurb: The albatross is a huge seabird that lives on and over the open Southern Ocean, with a few close cousins in the North Pacific. The wandering albatross has one of the largest wingspans of any living bird. Albatrosses come to land only to breed, on remote islands, and spend the rest of their lives at sea, where they fly enormous distances with very little effort. Their life history, their mating bonds, and the way they share parenting are all unusual by bird standards.
