arctic-tern.context_blurb: The Arctic tern is a small, slender white seabird that breeds in the Arctic summer and then flies to the Antarctic for the southern summer, following the sun to the other end of the planet. It is one of the most famous long-distance migrants on Earth, and tagging studies have measured just how far an individual tern actually travels in a lifetime. Everything about the Arctic tern's flight and timing is tuned to that one yearly commute.

bowerbird.context_blurb: Bowerbirds are a group of forest birds that live in New Guinea and Australia. The males are famous for one of the most elaborate courtship displays in the animal kingdom: they build an architectural stage on the forest floor and decorate it with carefully chosen objects to show off to visiting females. The bowers are not nests, and the arrangements the males make show real attention to color, pattern, and even perspective. Scientists treat bowerbirds as one of the clearest animal examples of something close to artistic effort.

cassowary.context_blurb: The cassowary is a tall, flightless rainforest bird that lives in northern Australia and New Guinea. It has a glossy black body, a brilliant blue neck, and a tall bony helmet on top of its head. Cassowaries can be dangerous when cornered, and their feet carry a specific weapon unusual in modern birds. The bird is also an important forest gardener, because a long list of rainforest trees depend on cassowaries to spread their seeds.

emperor-penguin.context_blurb: The emperor penguin is the largest penguin alive, standing about four feet tall. It lives only on the sea ice around Antarctica, which is also where it breeds in the middle of the worst winter on Earth. The emperor penguin raises its single chick through months of darkness and freezing wind by relying on a mix of parental teamwork, group behavior, and body chemistry that nothing else in the vertebrate world comes close to copying.

hummingbird.context_blurb: The hummingbird is a group of tiny, nectar-feeding birds that live only in the Americas. The smallest, the bee hummingbird of Cuba, weighs less than a penny. Hummingbirds have the fastest wingbeats of any bird, hover in place at flowers, and have the highest metabolism of any vertebrate for their size. All of these features drive a specific set of biology problems that hummingbird research keeps unpacking.

kiwi.context_blurb: The kiwi is a group of flightless, chicken-sized birds that live only in New Zealand. They are the national symbol of the country. Kiwis are nocturnal and have soft hair-like feathers, very poor eyesight, and a long flexible bill with nostrils at the tip. The nostrils-at-the-tip trick is almost unique among birds, and they are built around a very different kind of foraging than most of their flying cousins ever use.

lyrebird.context_blurb: The lyrebird is a large, ground-dwelling bird that lives in the forests of eastern Australia. The male has a long tail that fans up like a lyre in display. The lyrebird is one of the greatest vocal mimics in the natural world and can copy almost any sound it hears, including other birds, human machinery, and even camera shutters. The amount and precision of its mimicry is well-documented, and it has made the lyrebird a repeating star of nature documentaries.

new-caledonian-crow.context_blurb: The New Caledonian crow is a medium-sized black crow that lives only on a few islands in the southwest Pacific. It looks like any other crow at first glance, but it is one of the most skilled tool-using animals in the world. Researchers in Oxford and elsewhere have run careful experiments on these crows for decades. The results keep pushing bird cognition into territory most people associate with chimpanzees.

ostrich.context_blurb: The ostrich is the largest living bird on Earth, a flightless runner that lives on the savannas of Africa. An adult male can stand over nine feet tall. Ostriches cannot fly, but they can run faster than any other bird and defend themselves with a powerful kick. Their eggs, their eyes, and their lungs are all record-setters in their own ways. Ostriches are also still farmed in a number of countries for meat, leather, and feathers.

owl.context_blurb: The owl is a group of mostly nocturnal birds of prey found in every habitat on every continent except Antarctica. Owls combine almost silent flight, forward-facing eyes, and an extraordinary sense of hearing to hunt in near-total darkness. Each of those abilities depends on a specific anatomical feature not shared by most daytime raptors. Species of owl range from palm-sized elf owls to the Blakiston's fish owl, which has a wingspan close to six feet.

peregrine-falcon.context_blurb: The peregrine falcon is a widespread bird of prey found on every continent except Antarctica. It is best known for its hunting dive, which uses gravity to reach some of the fastest speeds ever measured in a living animal. Peregrines nearly went extinct across much of North America in the mid-twentieth century because of DDT contamination; they are now one of the most famous success stories of modern conservation. City skyscrapers in New York, Chicago, and London are now important peregrine nest sites.

shoebill.context_blurb: The shoebill is a huge, slate-grey wading bird that lives in the papyrus swamps of central and eastern Africa. It is one of the tallest wading birds in the world and has a gigantic shoe-shaped bill, from which it gets its name. Shoebills hunt by standing almost perfectly still for hours and then striking in a single motion that biologists have measured carefully. They are also famous for a specific sound they make instead of a call, and for a disturbing look at anyone who gets too close to their nest.

woodpecker.context_blurb: The woodpecker is a group of birds found in forests on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They are specialized tree-poundingclimbers with chisel-like beaks, stiff tails, and feet built for gripping bark. Woodpeckers hammer into wood at speeds and forces that would knock out any other bird's brain, and the way they manage to not get hurt is one of the most carefully studied puzzles in avian biomechanics.

17-year-cicada.context_blurb: The 17-year cicada is a large, red-eyed insect that lives in the forests of the eastern United States. Unlike most cicadas, this one spends its entire youth underground, sipping sap from tree roots in the dark for years at a time, before every member of a brood emerges at once in a single summer. The cicada's life history is one of the strangest timing problems in the insect world, and it has driven a lot of research on how prime numbers and group timing can be a survival strategy.

army-ants.context_blurb: Army ants are a group of ants that live in the tropical forests of the Americas, Africa, and Asia. Unlike most ants, they do not build permanent nests. Instead, the entire colony marches through the forest in long columns, overwhelms prey too big for any single ant to kill, and camps in a temporary living structure made from the bodies of the ants themselves. Army ant swarms are among the most dramatic ecological events in a tropical forest, and other animals have evolved to follow them for the stirred-up food.

bombardier-beetle.context_blurb: The bombardier beetle is a small ground beetle that lives on every continent except Antarctica. It is best known for a defensive weapon that is one of the most dramatic examples of chemical warfare in the animal kingdom. When attacked, the beetle fires something out of the tip of its abdomen, and it can aim it in any direction. The chemistry behind the explosion is still of ongoing research interest, and the beetle keeps turning up in debates about how such complicated systems evolve.

dragonfly.context_blurb: The dragonfly is a group of long-bodied flying insects that live near fresh water on every continent except Antarctica. The adults are expert fliers that can hover, dart, and reverse in a way no other insect family can match. Dragonflies spend most of their lives as aquatic larvae, which are themselves fierce underwater predators. Everything about the dragonfly, from its eyes to its wings to its hunting strategy, is tuned for catching other flying insects in open air.

dung-beetle.context_blurb: The dung beetle is a group of beetles that eat the droppings of larger animals and roll them into balls for food and breeding. They live on every continent except Antarctica. Dung beetles play a huge role in recycling nutrients in grasslands and farms around the world, and the ancient Egyptians treated them as sacred. Modern research keeps finding surprising things about how a dung beetle rolling a ball of dung knows where it is going.

firefly.context_blurb: The firefly is a kind of beetle that produces its own light in a pair of chemical-filled segments at the end of its abdomen. Fireflies live in warm, humid parts of every continent except Antarctica. On warm summer evenings, males fly over fields and forests flashing a species-specific pattern, while females wait in the grass and flash back. Modern biologists study the chemistry of firefly light for both its evolutionary story and its use in medical research.

hercules-beetle.context_blurb: The Hercules beetle is a huge rhinoceros beetle that lives in the rainforests of Central and South America. Males grow long, curved horns on their heads and bodies, which can be nearly as long as the rest of them. The Hercules beetle is one of the strongest animals on Earth relative to its body weight, and biologists sometimes use it as a benchmark when they are measuring how much an insect of a given size can lift or drag.

honeybee.context_blurb: The honeybee is a small, striped flying insect that lives in large colonies of thousands of workers, a handful of drones, and a single queen. The common honeybee was first domesticated in the Mediterranean thousands of years ago and is now kept all over the world. Honeybees are the most important crop pollinator of modern agriculture, and the way the colony makes decisions as a group, finds food, and defends its hive has made them one of the most carefully studied insects on Earth.

leafcutter-ants.context_blurb: Leafcutter ants are a group of ants that live in the tropical forests of Central and South America. They are famous for marching columns of workers each carrying a cut piece of leaf back to the nest. The ants do not actually eat the leaves. Instead, they use them to grow a crop in underground chambers, and the colony arrangement around that crop is one of the most striking cases of farming anywhere outside the human world.

monarch-butterfly.context_blurb: The monarch butterfly is a large orange-and-black butterfly that lives across North America, with populations in Mexico, the United States, and Canada. It is best known for one of the most famous animal migrations on Earth, a multi-generation journey between winter roost sites in central Mexico and summer breeding grounds far to the north. Monarchs are also chemically defended as caterpillars, and both of those features are at the heart of modern conservation efforts to save a species that has been declining fast.

peacock-spider.context_blurb: The peacock spider is a group of tiny jumping spiders that live mostly in Australia. The males fit on a fingernail, but they put on an elaborate visual courtship display that has made them an internet sensation. The dance is complicated enough that researchers have mapped out individual moves. For a species this small, the show is extraordinary.

praying-mantis.context_blurb: The praying mantis is a group of long, slender predatory insects found across most of the world, especially the tropics. They are named for the way they hold their folded forelegs together as they wait in ambush for other insects. Mantises have forward-facing eyes, extremely fast strike reflexes, and a famous courtship pattern that often makes it into high-school biology classrooms. They are the only insects that can turn their heads to look over their shoulders.

tardigrade.context_blurb: The tardigrade, also called a water bear or moss piglet, is a microscopic eight-legged animal that lives in mosses, lichens, and water puddles almost everywhere on Earth. Tardigrades are famous for surviving conditions that would kill almost any other animal, including the vacuum of space, deep radiation, and complete dehydration. The way they manage all this is still being worked out, and researchers have launched tardigrades on space missions on purpose to test the limits.

axolotl.context_blurb: The axolotl is a strange, feather-gilled salamander that lives only in a handful of lakes and canals around Mexico City. It is critically endangered in the wild, though millions are kept in laboratories and pet tanks around the world. The axolotl is famous for a peculiar life story: unlike almost every other salamander, it stays in a larval-looking form its whole life, keeps its gills, and never fully transforms. It also has one of the most studied regeneration systems in the whole animal kingdom.

chameleon.context_blurb: The chameleon is a group of mostly tree-dwelling lizards that live in Africa, Madagascar, southern Europe, and parts of Asia. They are famous for independently moving eyes, a long projectile tongue, and the ability to change color. Modern research has shown that the color change is tied as much to signaling as to camouflage, and the mechanism behind it turned out to be quite different from the simple pigment story that biology textbooks used to tell.

glass-frog.context_blurb: The glass frog is a group of small tree frogs that live in the rainforests of Central and South America. The undersides of their bodies are transparent, so if you turn one over you can see straight through the skin to the heart, liver, and digestive tract. The transparency is not an accident; it is a specific survival strategy that researchers have been unpacking with high-speed cameras and ultrasound, and the frog turns out to be hiding its blood during the day in a surprising way.

goliath-frog.context_blurb: The Goliath frog is the largest frog in the world, growing to the size of a small cat. It lives only in a narrow strip of fast-flowing rivers in the rainforests of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. The frog is in serious trouble because of hunting and habitat loss, and biologists are still learning how it reproduces. Recent fieldwork has shown that this huge frog does something to its own breeding environment that very few other frogs are known to do.

king-cobra.context_blurb: The king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world, a long, slender hooded snake that lives in the forests of South and Southeast Asia. Despite the name, it is not a true cobra; it belongs to its own genus. King cobras are specialists at eating other snakes, including other venomous ones. The female is also unusual among snakes for the way she treats her eggs, and the whole species has a far more carefully controlled lifestyle than its reputation suggests.

komodo-dragon.context_blurb: The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard, found only on a few small islands in Indonesia. Adults can exceed 10 feet in length and 150 pounds in weight. Komodos are ambush predators that take down deer, pigs, and even water buffalo, and they combine several nasty features in their bite that scientists are still sorting out. Their reproductive biology also has a quirk unusual for a vertebrate this size.

poison-dart-frog.context_blurb: Poison dart frogs are a group of small, brilliantly colored tree frogs that live in the rainforests of Central and South America. The colors are warnings: many species are among the most toxic animals on Earth, a few drops of their skin chemistry enough to kill much larger animals. Indigenous peoples of the Choco region of Colombia have used the toxins to tip blowgun darts for centuries. The chemistry turns out to come from the frog's diet, not from the frog itself.

saltwater-crocodile.context_blurb: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile and the largest crocodilian in the world. It lives in brackish waters from northern Australia and India east through Southeast Asia and the western Pacific. A saltie can swim long distances at sea and will cross large stretches of water between islands. It is one of the most dangerous animals to humans in its range, and its bite force is at the top end of anything ever measured in a vertebrate.

sea-turtle.context_blurb: The sea turtle is a group of large, long-lived marine turtles found in oceans around the world. All seven living species are classified as threatened or endangered. Sea turtles come ashore only to lay eggs, and most of their adult lives are spent swimming across huge ocean distances. Their navigation, their diet, and their long migratory routes are each the subject of major modern conservation projects.

tuatara.context_blurb: The tuatara is a lizard-shaped reptile that lives only on a few islands off the coast of New Zealand. It looks like a lizard, but it is not one; the tuatara is the only living member of an order of reptiles that otherwise died out around the same time as the dinosaurs. It has features of its skeleton, teeth, and even eye that have not changed in a very long time. Everything about the tuatara's slow life, from how long it takes to grow up to how long it lives, is on a scale almost unmatched among reptiles.

wood-frog.context_blurb: The wood frog is a small, dark-masked frog that lives in forests across much of Canada and the northern United States, farther north than any other North American amphibian. It survives winters that would kill every other North American frog by doing something to its own body that biologists find hard to believe the first time they read about it. The wood frog is one of the clearest living examples of how an animal can survive conditions that would otherwise be lethal.

dire-wolf.context_blurb: The dire wolf was a large wolf that lived across North America and into South America during the ice age, going extinct around 10,000 years ago. For a long time scientists thought it was closely related to living wolves, but 2021 DNA work surprised everyone and showed that its family placement is more distant than the fossils alone had suggested. Thousands of dire wolf skeletons have been pulled from the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles, which is one of the richest ice-age sites in the world.

giant-ground-sloth.context_blurb: The giant ground sloth is a group of huge, slow-moving ground mammals that lived across the Americas during the ice age, up to the end of the last glaciation about 10,000 years ago. The biggest of them, Megatherium, was the size of an elephant. These sloths were not the tree-dwellers of today; they were ground-dwelling browsers that stood on their back legs to pull down branches. Their disappearance is tied in with the same ice-age extinction debate that killed most of the other big American animals.

glyptodon.context_blurb: The glyptodon was a huge armored mammal that lived in South America during the ice age. It looked like a modern armadillo blown up to the size of a small car, with a solid, dome-shaped shell made of thousands of bony plates. Some species also had a club-tipped tail they could use in defense. Glyptodons went extinct around the same time most of the other large American animals disappeared, and recent DNA work has placed them firmly inside the modern armadillo family.

irish-elk-giant-deer.context_blurb: The Irish elk, more properly called the giant deer, was a huge deer that lived across Eurasia from the British Isles to central Russia during the ice age. The name is misleading: it was not an elk and was not confined to Ireland. The males of the species carried the largest antlers of any deer that ever lived, which is why so many well-preserved specimens have come out of Irish peat bogs. The giant deer went extinct between roughly 10,000 and 7,000 years ago.

mastodon.context_blurb: The mastodon was a huge elephant-like mammal that lived in the forests of North and Central America during the ice age and died out around 10,000 years ago. Despite looking like a mammoth, the mastodon belonged to a different family of elephant relatives. Its tusks, its teeth, and the way its molars were shaped are the clearest clues that it was a browser, not a grazer, and the differences from mammoths show up on almost every skeleton pulled out of a bog or quarry.

short-faced-bear.context_blurb: The short-faced bear was a huge bear that lived across North America during the ice age. Standing on its hind legs, it was taller than any living bear. The short-faced bear had long legs for its weight, a short snout, and a build that has split paleontologists into two camps about how it actually made a living. It went extinct around the end of the last ice age along with most of the other North American megafauna.

smilodon-saber-toothed-cat.context_blurb: Smilodon is the formal name for the most famous saber-toothed cat, a large, lion-sized predator that lived in the Americas during the ice age. It is not a close relative of any living cat and belongs to its own extinct branch of the cat family. Thousands of Smilodon skeletons have come out of the La Brea tar pits, which is where most of what scientists know about its anatomy and injuries comes from. Its two long upper canine teeth are the obvious signature feature, and biologists are still arguing about how exactly they were used.

terror-bird.context_blurb: The terror bird is the common name for a group of huge flightless predatory birds that lived in South America for most of the time after the dinosaurs. Some species stood nearly ten feet tall. Terror birds were the top land predators of their continent for millions of years before most of them went extinct. Their skulls, legs, and claws all point to a specific kind of hunting that paleontologists keep working to reconstruct in detail.

woolly-mammoth.context_blurb: The woolly mammoth was a huge, shaggy elephant-cousin that lived across the cold grasslands of Eurasia and North America during the ice age. Mammoths were close relatives of today's Asian elephant, with long curved tusks and a dense double coat for the deep cold. Most of them went extinct around the end of the last ice age, though a tiny isolated population survived on a remote Arctic island until a few thousand years ago. Frozen specimens have given paleontologists an unusually complete picture of the animal.

woolly-rhino.context_blurb: The woolly rhino was a shaggy, cold-adapted rhinoceros that lived across the cold grasslands of Eurasia during the ice age and died out around 10,000 years ago. It shared its range with mammoths and giant deer. Mummified and frozen specimens found in Siberia and Poland have given scientists a very detailed picture of its coat, its horn, and its diet, which was unusually specialized for a rhino. Ancient cave paintings in France and Spain show that early humans knew it well.

armor.context_blurb: Among animals, armor is any kind of built-in body shield that protects a creature from bites, claws, and blows. It can be scales, plates, shells, or thickened skin, and it has evolved separately in many different animal groups, from fish to mammals. Armor is almost never free: it slows an animal down, costs energy to grow, and limits how it can move. This topic looks at the specific designs animals have landed on across the natural world and the trade-offs each one has to accept.

chemical-weapons.context_blurb: Many animals defend themselves not with teeth or speed but with chemistry. Chemical weapons in animals range from mild irritants to deadly toxins, and from sprays, bites, and stings to secretions that soak into attackers' skin. Some animals make their own weapons; others steal theirs from their diet. This topic looks at how different animals produce, store, and deliver their chemical defenses, and what the chemistry does to a predator that gets a dose.

ditching-a-body-part-autotomy.context_blurb: A number of animals, from lizards and salamanders to spiders and sea cucumbers, can voluntarily drop a body part when a predator grabs it. The breaking is clean, bloodless, and the animal usually gets away. In some species the lost part grows back; in others it does not. Biologists call this trick autotomy, and this topic looks at the different ways animals use it, which parts they can afford to lose, and what trade-offs come with growing a replacement.

faking-it-mimicry.context_blurb: Mimicry is the trick of one animal looking, smelling, sounding, or acting like something else, usually to fool predators or prey. It shows up all over the natural world, from butterflies that match the pattern of a toxic species, to octopuses that imitate dangerous reef animals, to orchids that look like female wasps. This topic looks at the main families of mimicry biologists recognize, how each one works, and how a species ends up locked into looking like another one.

playing-dead-tonic-immobility.context_blurb: Many animals, from possums to beetles to sharks, respond to serious threats by freezing up and faking death. The trick is called tonic immobility, and it is more than just lying still: the animal's whole body chemistry and reflexes change, often enough to fool a predator into letting go. This topic looks at which animals use tonic immobility, how it is triggered, and why for some predators, a limp meal is less interesting than a struggling one.

safety-in-numbers.context_blurb: Many animals live in big groups because big groups are safer than being alone. Schools of fish, flocks of starlings, herds of wildebeest, and swarms of insects all use some combination of numbers, patterns, and coordinated motion to confuse or exhaust predators. This topic looks at the different ways animals use groups for safety, from the simple statistics of being one target in a crowd to the specific tricks a predator has to deal with when thousands move at once.

spines-and-quills.context_blurb: Many animals carry spines, quills, or sharp bristles for defense. Porcupines, hedgehogs, sea urchins, and pufferfish all use variations on the same idea: make yourself hard to swallow by sticking something sharp in whatever tries. The structures vary from barbed hairs to actual bony spines, and the way they are deployed varies by species. This topic looks at the specific designs different animal groups have landed on and what each one costs.

vanishing-camouflage-and-active-color-ch.context_blurb: Camouflage lets an animal disappear into its background. It can be as simple as a fixed color pattern that matches a specific environment, or as sophisticated as a cephalopod's skin changing pattern, color, and texture in a fraction of a second. This topic covers both kinds, from the quiet static camouflage of a stick insect or a stonefish to the active, changing camouflage of octopuses and flatfish, and the sensory machinery each kind depends on.

wearing-a-warning-aposematism.context_blurb: Some animals do the opposite of camouflage: instead of hiding, they wear bright, bold colors that advertise the fact that they taste bad, sting, or are toxic. Biologists call this aposematism, and the strategy only works when predators learn to associate the signal with a bad experience. Poison dart frogs, monarch butterflies, skunks, and coral snakes all use some version of warning signaling, and this topic looks at how the signal has to be loud, consistent, and backed up by a real cost to the attacker.

all-in-vs-none-parental-investment.context_blurb: Animals handle parenting in two very different ways. Some, like whales, elephants, and humans, have very few young at a time and pour huge amounts of effort into each one. Others, like many fish and insects, produce enormous numbers of offspring and leave them to fend for themselves. Biologists call the trade-off between these strategies parental investment, and this topic looks at the different corners of it that different animals have landed in and why neither extreme is always the right answer.

eggs-vs-live-birth.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, there are two main ways to produce offspring: lay eggs or give birth to live young. Fish, reptiles, amphibians, insects, and nearly all birds lay eggs, while most mammals carry young inside the body. The split is not quite as clean as that, though: some reptiles are live-bearers, a few mammals still lay eggs, and some sharks have internal eggs that hatch before birth. This topic looks at the specific trade-offs each strategy carries.

insect-super-societies-eusociality.context_blurb: A few insect groups live in enormous, highly organized societies. Honeybees, ants, termites, and some wasps all have a single reproductive female, large numbers of non-breeding workers, and sometimes specialized soldier castes. Biologists call this arrangement eusociality. This topic looks at how eusocial insects divide labor, defend their nests, and raise young, and at how such an elaborate social system evolved out of simpler nesting arrangements more than once.

metamorphosis.context_blurb: Many animals do not grow by simply getting bigger. Insects, frogs, and sea stars go through metamorphosis, a dramatic transformation from one body plan to a completely different one between their young and adult stages. A caterpillar becoming a butterfly is the most famous example, but the trick shows up all over the animal kingdom. This topic looks at the different kinds of metamorphosis, how the body remakes itself inside a cocoon or pupa, and why it is useful enough to be worth all the risk.

pouches-and-tiny-newborns-marsupials.context_blurb: Marsupials are a group of mammals that give birth to tiny, barely-formed young and finish raising them outside the body, usually in a pouch. The group lives mostly in Australia and the Americas and includes kangaroos, koalas, opossums, wombats, and Tasmanian devils. This topic looks at the specific parenting arrangement marsupials use, how the newborn makes its way to the pouch, and why this very different strategy has stayed competitive against the placental mammals that took over most of the rest of the world.

showing-off-to-win-a-mate-sexual-selecti.context_blurb: A huge amount of the strangest-looking features in the animal kingdom come from the problem of attracting a mate. Peacock tails, bird-of-paradise dances, elk antlers, firefly flashes, and bowerbird bowers all exist because the opposite sex pays attention to them. Biologists call this sexual selection. This topic looks at the different flavors of it, from direct combat between rivals to displays that cost the showoff energy or safety, and the surprising places it keeps turning up in nature.

switching-sex.context_blurb: A number of animals, including many fish, some shrimp, and certain reef invertebrates, can change their biological sex during their lifetime. The direction of the change, when it happens, and what triggers it vary from group to group. Clownfish and wrasses are two famous examples that work in opposite directions. This topic looks at the main patterns scientists recognize, the ecological situations that favor each one, and the surprising social details that drive the switch in some reef communities.

virgin-birth-parthenogenesis.context_blurb: In a handful of animal species, females can produce offspring without any input from a male. Biologists call this parthenogenesis. It is common among some lizards, insects, and crustaceans, and it has been documented in a few surprising places, including sharks, snakes, and birds in captivity. This topic looks at how parthenogenesis works at the genetic level, what triggers it in species that can do both options, and the specific trade-offs that come with reproducing without a partner.

ankylosaurus.context_blurb: Ankylosaurus was a large, armored herbivorous dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America at the very end of the age of the dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. It was a slow, low-slung quadruped with a body the shape of a tank: its back was covered in bony plates and spikes, and its tail ended in a solid mass of fused bone. Everything about Ankylosaurus is a specific response to living alongside huge meat-eating dinosaurs, and its design keeps turning up in paleontology textbooks as a classic case of armored dinosaur.

archaeopteryx.context_blurb: Archaeopteryx is a famous feathered dinosaur that lived in what is now southern Germany about 150 million years ago, in the late Jurassic. It had feathers like a bird but a long bony tail, teeth, and hand bones like a dinosaur. When the first Archaeopteryx fossil was found in the 1860s, just two years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species, it became one of the single most important fossils in evolutionary biology. It is the clearest early link between dinosaurs and today's birds.

argentinosaurus.context_blurb: Argentinosaurus is one of the largest land animals that ever existed. It was a long-necked sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Patagonia, Argentina, about 95 million years ago. Only a few bones have ever been found, and paleontologists have had to estimate its size and weight from pieces of its backbone and leg. Everything about Argentinosaurus is at the limit of what a land animal's skeleton, heart, and lungs can support, and researchers keep returning to it as a benchmark for how big a dinosaur can get.

spinosaurus.context_blurb: Spinosaurus was a very large meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now North Africa about 95 million years ago. It had a long, narrow, crocodile-like snout and a tall sail of bony spines along its back. For most of the twentieth century, Spinosaurus was known only from a single partial skeleton that was destroyed in World War II. Modern discoveries in Morocco have now shown that this dinosaur was shaped unlike any other big theropod and probably made its living in a very different way.

stegosaurus.context_blurb: Stegosaurus was a large plant-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America about 150 million years ago. It is one of the most instantly recognizable dinosaurs, with two rows of tall plates down its back and a cluster of long spikes on its tail. Paleontologists are still working on exactly what the plates were for and how they were arranged in life. Its small head and tiny brain have also made it a repeating character in debates about dinosaur intelligence.

triceratops.context_blurb: Triceratops was a large horned dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America at the very end of the age of the dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. It is one of the most familiar dinosaurs, with a huge bony frill behind its head and three horns above the face. Triceratops lived at the same time as Tyrannosaurus rex, and their remains sometimes turn up in the same formations. This topic looks at the specific features that make Triceratops a classic ceratopsian.

tyrannosaurus-rex.context_blurb: Tyrannosaurus rex was a huge meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America at the very end of the age of the dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. It is the most famous dinosaur in the world. Modern paleontology has reshaped the picture of T. rex considerably in the last few decades, from its bite force to its posture to the small size of its arms to whether it had feathers. This topic looks at the specific details that current evidence actually supports.

velociraptor.context_blurb: Velociraptor was a small, feathered meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now Mongolia and northern China about 75 to 71 million years ago. The real Velociraptor was closer in size to a large turkey than to the people-sized predators in Jurassic Park. It had a long stiff tail, a brain unusually large for its body size, and a long curved claw on each foot that paleontologists have been studying with CT scans and physics models to work out how it was actually used.

basking-shark-cetorhinus-maximus.context_blurb: The basking shark is a huge, slow-moving shark that lives in temperate oceans around the world. It is the second-largest fish in the world, after the whale shark. Unlike most sharks, it is a filter feeder on tiny plankton rather than a hunter of large prey. Basking sharks gather in large numbers in a few predictable places off the coasts of the United Kingdom and the northeastern United States, and researchers use those gatherings to track them.

cookiecutter-shark-isistius-brasiliensis.context_blurb: The cookiecutter shark is a small, cigar-shaped deep-sea shark that lives throughout the world's tropical oceans. It is less than two feet long but has one of the most unusual feeding methods of any vertebrate. The cookiecutter shark cannot eat big animals whole, so instead it attaches to them and takes a single circular bite out of their flesh. The holes it leaves show up on whales, dolphins, large fish, and even submarines, which is partly how biologists worked out what it does for a living.

frilled-shark-chlamydoselachus-anguineus.context_blurb: The frilled shark is a long, eel-shaped shark that lives in the deep ocean around much of the world. It is named for the six pairs of frilly gill slits around its throat. The frilled shark has an unusually long, snaky body for a shark, and its teeth are shaped like tiny forks. The animal is sometimes called a living fossil because its lineage is extremely old and its body plan has features that modern sharks have mostly lost.

goblin-shark-mitsukurina-owstoni.context_blurb: The goblin shark is a strange, pink-skinned, deep-sea shark that lives in warm waters around the world but is best known in Japan. It has a long, flattened snout like a sword, small eyes, and a jaw that can launch forward out of its head in a way few other sharks can match. The jaw mechanics are the single most-studied thing about the species, because they are so different from any other living fish.

greenland-shark-somniosus-microcephalus.context_blurb: The Greenland shark is a huge, slow, cold-water shark that lives in the deep cold waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans. It grows to over 20 feet long and is one of the longest-lived vertebrates in the world, with some individuals believed to be several centuries old. The flesh of the Greenland shark contains chemistry that is toxic to humans unless prepared very specifically. Everything about this shark's life, from how slowly it swims to how long it takes to mature, is on an unusually slow timescale.

sawfish-pristidae.context_blurb: The sawfish is a group of large, flat-bodied rays with long, saw-like extensions of the snout. They live in warm, shallow coastal waters and estuaries around the world, with especially important populations in northern Australia and the southern United States. Sawfish are among the most critically endangered marine animals, mainly because of fishing pressure and the loss of coastal nurseries. The saw is not just for show; the sawfish uses it to hunt in a specific way scientists have worked out from both tank and field studies.

thresher-shark-alopias.context_blurb: The thresher shark is a group of long-tailed sharks that live in temperate and tropical oceans around the world. The upper lobe of the tail is nearly as long as the rest of the body. Threshers are specialists in hunting schools of small fish, and the way they use that long tail in the hunt is a dramatic example of a shark using its body as more than just a swimming machine. High-speed filming by researchers off the Philippines captured the behavior clearly.

wobbegong-orectolobidae-carpet-sharks.context_blurb: The wobbegong is a group of flat, patterned carpet sharks that live mostly on the reefs around Australia and the Indo-Pacific. They are camouflaged so well against the coral and sand that divers often swim right over one without seeing it. The wobbegong has a wide, fringe-edged mouth and acts as an ambush hunter rather than a chaser. Its body plan is unlike almost any other shark's, and the fringed camouflage keeps appearing in textbooks on how a predator can hide in plain sight.

beaks-for-every-meal.context_blurb: A bird's beak is a precision tool, and across the bird world almost every meal has driven a specific beak shape. Finches crack seeds, hummingbirds reach into flowers, flamingos filter plankton upside down, pelicans scoop fish, and parrots crack hard nuts. This topic looks at the way beak shape, size, and strength are tied to a bird's diet, and at the famous Galapagos finch studies that showed those shapes can shift measurably over just a few generations.

digesting-grass-the-ruminants-four-stoma.context_blurb: Grass is one of the most abundant foods on land and one of the hardest to digest. Cows, sheep, goats, deer, and giraffes handle grass by using a multi-chambered stomach and a long partnership with a huge community of microbes. This topic looks at the specific anatomy of ruminant digestion, how the animal chews and re-chews its food, and why this is a slow but surprisingly efficient way to make a living on a diet of pure plant fiber.

filter-feeding-the-ocean.context_blurb: Many of the largest animals in the sea live by sieving tiny food out of enormous volumes of water. Blue whales, whale sharks, basking sharks, flamingos, and sponges all use some form of filter feeding. This topic looks at the different ways animals do it, from the baleen in a whale's mouth to the specialized gill rakers in a whale shark, and at how such a dilute food source can still support animals the size of a city bus.

lures-and-ambush.context_blurb: Many predators do not chase prey; they wait and let prey come to them. Anglerfish, snapping turtles, trapdoor spiders, antlions, and even some snakes use some form of lure or ambush. This topic looks at the different mechanical and visual tricks animals use to attract prey into striking range, and at the sensory machinery an ambush predator needs to make the final strike in a single, very fast motion.

remarkable-tongues.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, tongues do a lot more than taste. Chameleons shoot their tongues like projectiles. Anteaters, aardvarks, and pangolins use theirs as living fly-swatters for ants. Nectar-feeding bats and butterflies carry absurdly long tongues for the bottoms of flowers. This topic looks at the specific tongue designs different animals have landed on and the trade-offs each one brings along.

squeezing-not-biting.context_blurb: A number of snakes and some other predators kill their prey not with venom or teeth but by wrapping around them and squeezing. Boas, pythons, and anacondas are the most famous constrictors. This topic looks at the specific mechanics of constriction, which modern research has shown is more subtle than the simple crushing-the-lungs story most textbooks used to tell, and at the specific body shape and muscle arrangement a constricting predator needs.

teeth-built-for-the-job.context_blurb: Teeth are a mammalian specialty, and different mammal groups carry very different sets of them. Carnivores have scissor-like molars for shearing meat, herbivores have broad grinding molars for plants, and omnivores like us have a mix. This topic looks at how tooth shape reveals a mammal's diet, and how specific specialists, from sharks with endless replacement teeth to narwhals with a single long tusk, have taken the basic tooth design in extreme directions.

venom-for-the-hunt.context_blurb: Many predators carry venom for subduing prey, not just for defense. Snakes, spiders, scorpions, cone snails, cephalopods, and even a handful of mammals use chemistry to kill or paralyze prey too dangerous to subdue any other way. This topic looks at the different venom delivery systems different animal groups have evolved, how venoms work in the body of the prey, and why nature keeps re-inventing the same basic trick across lineages that are not even remotely related.

blue-whale.context_blurb: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth, bigger than any dinosaur ever recorded. An adult blue whale can be nearly 100 feet long and weigh close to 200 tons. Blue whales live in every ocean and feed almost exclusively on tiny shrimp-like crustaceans called krill. Their huge size, their songs, and the way they pump krill through plates of baleen in a single enormous mouthful are all tightly linked parts of the same ecological strategy.

dolphin.context_blurb: Dolphins are a group of highly intelligent marine mammals that live in oceans and some rivers worldwide. They are small toothed whales, closely related to orcas and sperm whales. Dolphins hunt in coordinated groups, communicate with a complex set of calls, and use a specialized sense that lets them detect prey in dark or murky water. Modern research has shown they also have unusually complex social lives for a non-primate, including signature identifiers for individual members of a pod.

humpback-whale.context_blurb: The humpback whale is a huge baleen whale that lives in oceans worldwide, famous for its long migrations, its acrobatic breaching, and the complex songs sung by males on breeding grounds. Humpbacks are filter feeders that use specific cooperative hunting techniques few other whales share, and they interact with other species in surprising ways on the surface. The songs change season by season and whale by whale, and researchers have been tracking those changes for decades.

narwhal.context_blurb: The narwhal is a medium-sized Arctic whale, best known for the single long spiral tusk growing out of the front of the males' heads. Narwhals live year-round in the icy waters of the Arctic Ocean, mostly off Canada, Greenland, and Russia. The tusk is actually a modified tooth, and biologists have been working out what it is really for using a mix of DNA sampling, careful observation, and some surprising high-tech measurements of its surface sensitivity.

orca-killer-whale.context_blurb: The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of the dolphin family and lives in every ocean on Earth. Despite the name, orcas are not whales in the usual sense. They are highly intelligent toothed predators that live in family groups with their own hunting techniques, prey preferences, and vocal dialects. Different orca populations behave almost like different species, and researchers now think of them in terms of distinct ecotypes with different cultures and genetics.

sea-otter.context_blurb: The sea otter is a small marine mammal that lives in the cold coastal waters of the North Pacific, from California to Alaska and across to Russia and Japan. Unlike most marine mammals, it does not have a layer of blubber for insulation. Instead, it has the densest fur of any animal on Earth, which it keeps meticulously groomed. Sea otters also do something with their forepaws that few other marine mammals do, and the ecosystem they live in depends on it.

sperm-whale.context_blurb: The sperm whale is a huge toothed whale with a square-shaped head and the largest brain of any animal that has ever lived on Earth. Sperm whales live in oceans around the world and dive to astonishing depths to hunt large deep-sea prey. They are also famous for a dense waxy substance in their heads that whalers hunted them nearly to extinction for during the nineteenth century. Everything about their diving, their calls, and their social structure is on a huge scale.

walrus.context_blurb: The walrus is a huge, tusked marine mammal that lives in cold shallow seas around the Arctic. Both males and females grow long ivory tusks. Walruses haul out on ice floes and beaches in large herds, feed on bottom-dwelling clams and sea invertebrates, and use their tusks and whiskers together as a specialized set of tools. Climate change is now rapidly reshaping the ice cover they depend on.

growing-by-molting-the-exoskeleton-probl.context_blurb: Animals with hard external skeletons, from crabs to insects to spiders, cannot simply get bigger the way a mammal does. Instead, they have to shed and rebuild their whole outer shell every so often, in a dangerous process called molting. This topic looks at how molting works, what happens to the animal while its new shell is still soft, and what trade-offs come with wearing your skeleton on the outside instead of on the inside.

radial-vs-bilateral-why-a-jellyfish-has-.context_blurb: Most familiar animals have a clear front and back, a left and right that mirror each other, and a head that leads the body. Biologists call this bilateral symmetry. Some animals, including jellyfish, sea stars, and sea anemones, do not; they are organized around a central axis instead, with no obvious head. This topic looks at the two basic plans, how each one shapes an animal's lifestyle, and why bilateral animals ended up dominating most environments.

the-big-invertebrate-groups.context_blurb: The animal kingdom is overwhelmingly made up of invertebrates, animals without a backbone. The big invertebrate groups include arthropods, mollusks, cnidarians, echinoderms, and annelid worms. This topic looks at what makes each group distinct, how biologists tell them apart, and what the most famous animals in each group have in common with the lesser-known members of their family. Vertebrates like us are a tiny slice of the total animal picture.

the-five-vertebrate-classes-the-recognit.context_blurb: The vertebrates, animals with a backbone, are usually sorted into five big living classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. This topic walks through how biologists tell the five apart, what the key features of each one are, and the places where the lines get blurrier than textbooks suggest. The idea that each class has a tidy definition is useful for a 10th-grade reader but hides some real surprises in modern taxonomy.

the-rule-breakers-monotremes-and-marsupi.context_blurb: Most mammals carry their young inside the body and give birth to live, fully-formed babies. Monotremes and marsupials are the exceptions. Monotremes, which include the platypus and echidnas, still lay eggs; marsupials, including kangaroos, koalas, and opossums, give birth to tiny, barely-formed young that finish developing outside the body. This topic looks at these two rule-breaking groups and why they are so important for understanding what being a mammal really means.

what-makes-a-bird.context_blurb: Birds are the only living animals with feathers, and feathers are the single most useful feature for picking a bird out of a lineup. But birds also share a specific body plan: a toothless beak, hollow bones, a large keeled breastbone, and air-sac lungs. This topic walks through the main features that make a bird a bird, which of them show up elsewhere in the animal kingdom, and how birds inherited their key traits from a specific group of dinosaurs.

what-makes-a-mammal.context_blurb: Mammals are a diverse group of animals that includes everything from mice to blue whales. All of them share a specific set of features: hair, milk-producing mammary glands, three middle-ear bones, and a four-chambered heart. This topic looks at the key features that define a mammal, how biologists use them to tell mammals apart from the other vertebrate groups, and the handful of mammal species that break the usual rules in surprising ways.

what-makes-a-reptile-an-amphibian-dry-sc.context_blurb: Reptiles and amphibians are easy to confuse at first glance, but they are two very different animal groups. Reptiles, including snakes, lizards, turtles, and crocodilians, have dry scaly skin and lay shelled eggs on land. Amphibians, including frogs, salamanders, and caecilians, have soft moist skin and mostly lay unshelled eggs in water. This topic looks at the key features that separate the two groups and why the differences are more than just skin-deep.

antifreeze-blood-and-freezing-solid.context_blurb: Some animals can survive temperatures well below freezing, either by keeping their body liquid with chemistry that works like antifreeze, or by letting themselves freeze solid and surviving the thaw. Arctic fish, certain frogs, several insects, and tardigrades all handle sub-zero cold in different ways. This topic looks at the chemistry and the specific body changes that let an animal cheat the physics of ice forming inside living cells.

coming-back-from-dry-death-cryptobiosis.context_blurb: A handful of very tough animals, including tardigrades, nematode worms, and some rotifers, can survive near-total drying out and come back to life when they get wet again. Biologists call this cryptobiosis. This topic looks at how an animal can seemingly stop almost all life processes, suspend itself for years or even decades, and then wake up when conditions improve. The chemistry involved is still an active area of research.

heat-exchange-plumbing-countercurrent.context_blurb: Many animals use a specific plumbing trick in their blood vessels to save heat or to cool themselves. By running incoming blood right next to outgoing blood in opposite directions, they recycle heat before it is lost. Penguins, tuna, dolphins, and desert mammals all use some version of this countercurrent arrangement. This topic looks at how the trick works and the different problems different animals have used it to solve.

living-without-water.context_blurb: Some animals almost never drink water. Desert rodents like kangaroo rats, camels, and a handful of insects extract nearly all the water they need from their food and metabolism. This topic looks at the specific body chemistry, kidney function, and behavior that let an animal keep its tissues wet in an environment where free water is almost always out of reach.

size-ears-and-heat-radiators-and-bergman.context_blurb: Animals in cold climates tend to be larger and more compact, while animals in hot climates tend to be smaller and have longer limbs and ears. The pattern is called Bergmann's and Allen's rules, and it is tied to a simple physics problem about surface area and volume. This topic looks at how the rules play out in real animals, where they break, and how body parts like elephant ears or fennec fox ears work as built-in radiators.

sleeping-through-winter-hibernation-and-.context_blurb: A number of mammals and a few other animals get through winter by lowering their body temperature and metabolism and sleeping it off. The deepest version is hibernation, used by ground squirrels and marmots among others; a shallower version, torpor, is used daily by hummingbirds and some bats. This topic looks at what the body does during these shutdowns, how it protects itself from damage, and why only some animals have this strategy available.

the-two-engines-warm-blooded-vs-cold-blo.context_blurb: Vertebrates split roughly into two groups by the way they manage body temperature. Mammals and birds burn food fast to generate their own body heat, which lets them stay active in the cold but costs a lot of food. Fish, reptiles, and amphibians rely on the sun and the surrounding environment, which is cheaper but much more dependent on weather. This topic looks at the trade-offs each strategy brings and the animals that blur the line between the two.

compound-eyes-and-the-insect-mosaic.context_blurb: Insects and most other arthropods see with compound eyes, which are made of thousands of tiny individual lenses packed together into a single large eye. Each lens points in a slightly different direction, and the brain pieces the signals into a mosaic image. This topic looks at how a compound eye works, what it is good at, where it falls short, and why evolution has kept this design going in insects for hundreds of millions of years.

eyeshine-and-seeing-in-the-dark.context_blurb: Many nocturnal animals, including cats, raccoons, owls, and crocodiles, have eyes that shine when a light hits them in the dark. The glow is a side effect of a specific trick these animals use to see better in the gloom. This topic looks at that trick, which animal groups have it, which do not, and why it is one of the simplest and most useful upgrades to a vertebrate eye.

focusing-light-underwater.context_blurb: Underwater vision is a different problem from vision in air. The physics of light changes at the surface, so a fish's eye focuses in a different way than ours does. This topic looks at how fish, octopuses, and marine mammals solve the problem of making a sharp image underwater, and what happens when an animal, like a diving bird, has to see clearly in both worlds.

predator-eyes-vs-prey-eyes.context_blurb: Most predators have forward-facing eyes that give them good depth perception for pouncing, while most prey animals have eyes on the sides of the head that give them wide fields of view. The pattern shows up in cats versus rabbits, hawks versus doves, and across most of the vertebrate world. This topic looks at the specific trade-offs between depth and breadth, and at the animals that mix the two in interesting ways.

seeing-colors-we-cant-ultraviolet.context_blurb: Many animals, including birds, bees, and a surprising number of fish and reptiles, see in parts of the spectrum that human eyes cannot pick up. The most common extension is into the ultraviolet. This topic looks at which animals have UV vision, what they use it for, and why some human-visible flowers and bird feathers look very different when photographed in UV light.

the-mantis-shrimp-color-myth.context_blurb: The mantis shrimp has 12 to 16 types of color-receiving cells in its eyes, far more than our 3. For years, popular science articles reported that this means the shrimp sees many more colors than humans can imagine. More recent experiments have shown that the real story is subtler than that. This topic looks at what mantis shrimp vision actually does and does not do, and why their eyes are still some of the most unusual in the whole animal kingdom.

the-strangest-eyes-in-the-animal-kingdom.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, eyes have been invented and reinvented many different times. Some animals see through pinholes, some through mirrors, some through compound arrays, some through transparent heads. This topic looks at the strangest eye designs biologists know of, from scallops' hundreds of little blue eyes around their shells to the enormous eye of a colossal squid, and at what each design is actually doing for the animal that carries it.

anomalocaris.context_blurb: Anomalocaris was a large, strange swimming predator that lived in the Cambrian seas more than 500 million years ago. It had a soft body, two long grasping appendages on its face, a mouth made of overlapping plates, and a set of swimming flaps along both sides of its body. For decades, paleontologists thought the pieces of its body were parts of several different unrelated animals; it took careful work to put the picture back together. Anomalocaris was the top predator of its time and one of the most famous animals of the Burgess Shale.

arthropleura.context_blurb: Arthropleura was a giant millipede-like arthropod that lived in the forests of what is now Europe and North America during the Carboniferous period, around 300 million years ago. Some specimens were more than two meters long, which may make Arthropleura the largest land invertebrate that has ever lived. The oxygen-rich atmosphere of the Carboniferous may be part of the reason why. This topic looks at how such a huge arthropod could have made a living on the forest floor.

hallucigenia.context_blurb: Hallucigenia is a bizarre little animal from the Cambrian seas of what is now British Columbia, more than 500 million years ago. It had a tube-shaped body, pairs of long spines on its back, and pairs of soft legs underneath. When it was first described in the 1970s, paleontologists had its spikes on the bottom and its legs on top, and even its head and tail were later found to be reversed. Hallucigenia has become a famous example of how hard it is to reconstruct a soft-bodied Cambrian animal from scratch.

meganeura.context_blurb: Meganeura was a huge dragonfly-like insect that lived in the forests of what is now Europe during the Carboniferous period, around 300 million years ago. Its wingspan reached about two and a half feet, making it one of the largest flying insects that has ever lived. Oxygen levels in the Carboniferous atmosphere were higher than today, which may be part of why insects could grow so large. This topic looks at how an insect this size could even stay airborne.

opabinia.context_blurb: Opabinia was a strange little swimming animal from the Cambrian seas of what is now British Columbia, more than 500 million years ago. It had five eyes on top of its head and a long flexible nozzle on the front of its face. When the first careful reconstruction of Opabinia was shown at a scientific meeting in 1972, the audience reportedly laughed, assuming it was a joke. It is now one of the most famous animals of the Cambrian explosion.

trilobites.context_blurb: Trilobites were a huge group of marine arthropods that lived in the oceans for more than 270 million years, from the Cambrian explosion to the great end-Permian extinction. There were tens of thousands of species, in a huge range of sizes and shapes. Trilobites are among the most common animal fossils in the world and are a favorite of amateur paleontologists. Their eyes, their hard shells, and the way they molted have all left extraordinary records in rock.

growing-it-back-regeneration.context_blurb: Many animals can regrow lost body parts, but how much they can regrow varies hugely. Starfish can regrow an entire body from a single arm; salamanders can regrow whole limbs; lizards can regrow their tails but not their limbs. Mammals, including us, can only regrow a very limited set of tissues. This topic looks at the different animal groups and how far their regeneration goes.

living-fast-dying-young-the-mayflys-sing.context_blurb: Mayflies are a group of flying insects that live for years as aquatic larvae and emerge as adults for a very short period, sometimes only a single day. During that short adult life, mayflies have no working mouthparts and do nothing but mate and lay eggs. This topic looks at the strange schedule of a mayfly's life and at the specific trade-offs that come with putting almost all of life into one window of time.

not-dying-of-old-age-the-immortal-jellyf.context_blurb: A tiny jellyfish called Turritopsis dohrnii, native to the Mediterranean and found around the world as a stowaway on ships, can rewind its life back to an earlier stage when it is injured or stressed. In theory, it never has to die of old age. In practice, almost all of them do get eaten or killed by disease, so the trick is more interesting biologically than it is practically. This topic looks at how the rewinding actually works at the cellular level.

the-great-migrations.context_blurb: A number of animals cover huge distances every year as part of their life cycle. Some seabirds fly nearly pole to pole, monarch butterflies migrate across generations between Mexico and Canada, wildebeest circle the Serengeti, and salmon return to the specific streams where they were born. This topic looks at the different ways animals navigate and the specific pressures that make this kind of long-distance commute worth the energy.

the-oldest-animals-alive.context_blurb: Some animals are extraordinarily long-lived. Certain cold-water sharks are thought to live more than 400 years. Bowhead whales reach well over 200. Ocean quahog clams can live more than 500 years, and glass sponges may live for several thousand. This topic looks at the oldest-known individuals among living animals, how researchers age them, and what they share about how biological aging can be slowed.

learning-a-voice-vocal-mimicry-and-learn.context_blurb: A small group of animals, including parrots, songbirds, mockingbirds, lyrebirds, dolphins, and even a few elephants, learn their vocal signals rather than being born knowing them. Vocal learning is actually quite rare in the animal kingdom, and it shares some surprising brain-wiring features with human speech. This topic looks at the animals that have cracked the vocal-learning problem and the ways researchers test what they are actually doing with it.

making-light-bioluminescence.context_blurb: Many animals produce their own light. Fireflies flash to find mates, deep-sea anglerfish dangle glowing lures, dinoflagellates light up ocean waves, and jellyfish sparkle when disturbed. Biologists call this bioluminescence, and the chemistry behind it is surprisingly similar across very distant lineages. This topic looks at the different ways animals use light and the common chemical tricks that keep showing up in nature.

recognizing-yourself-the-mirror-test.context_blurb: In a classic experiment, a researcher puts a mark on an animal and shows it a mirror. If the animal uses the mirror to notice and investigate the mark on its own body, biologists say it has passed the mirror test, which is one standard way of asking whether an animal has some sense of itself. Great apes, elephants, dolphins, orcas, magpies, and more recently a particular cleaner fish have all passed in some form. This topic looks at what the test does and does not prove.

the-waggle-dance-how-a-bee-maps-the-flow.context_blurb: When a honeybee finds a good food source, she returns to the hive and performs a specific sequence of movements on the comb that tells her nestmates where to go. Other bees are able to read those movements accurately enough to fly to the right flower patch. The behavior was decoded in the mid-twentieth century by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who later won a Nobel Prize for the work, and it remains one of the clearest examples of a non-human communication system that encodes real information.

tool-users.context_blurb: A number of animals, from chimpanzees and sea otters to crows and octopuses, use tools in the wild. Some use sticks, some use stones, some use shells, and a few even make tools from scratch rather than just picking them up. This topic looks at the main tool-using species biologists study, what each one actually does, and how the definition of tool use has become more careful over the last several decades of fieldwork.

air-breathers-in-water-lungs-where-youd-.context_blurb: Several fish and amphibians breathe air at the surface, even though they live in water. Lungfish, snakeheads, bettas, and gars all have some form of lung or lung-like organ. The strategy pays off in warm, oxygen-poor water, where gills alone cannot pull enough oxygen out of the water. This topic looks at the specific body features different air-breathing fish have evolved and at how these animals handle the double problem of being an aquatic animal that still has to come up for air.

breathing-water-how-gills-pull-oxygen-fr.context_blurb: Fish and many invertebrates breathe by pulling oxygen out of water with gills. Gills look simple, but they are a sophisticated plumbing system: water flows past a dense feathery surface stuffed with blood vessels, and oxygen crosses from the water into the blood in a very specific way. This topic looks at how gills actually work, why they have to be arranged the way they are, and the specific trick fish use to pull oxygen out of water that already has very little of it.

extraordinary-hearts-and-blood.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, hearts and blood come in many strange forms. Octopuses have three hearts, giraffes have the highest-pressure hearts of any mammal, and icefish have no red blood cells at all. Some invertebrates even run on blood that is not red. This topic looks at the specific circulatory tricks different animals have landed on and the physics problems each one solves.

why-insects-cant-be-giant-the-tracheae-p.context_blurb: Insects breathe through a network of tiny tubes called tracheae that run from pores in the body wall directly to the tissues. The system is efficient at small sizes, but it does not scale up: the tubes have to get wider as an insect gets bigger, and at some point they take up so much room that there is nothing left for muscle. This topic looks at the physics and anatomy of why no modern insect gets as big as the giant Carboniferous ones ever did.

archaeopteryx-dinosaur-becomes-bird.context_blurb: Archaeopteryx is a famous feathered dinosaur that lived in what is now southern Germany about 150 million years ago. It is a textbook transitional fossil, with features of both dinosaurs and today's birds: feathers and a wishbone on the one hand; teeth and a bony tail on the other. This topic looks at exactly which features in Archaeopteryx make the dinosaur-to-bird transition visible in a single animal's skeleton.

our-hominin-cousins-neanderthal-and-deni.context_blurb: Modern humans are not the only humans who have lived on Earth. Neanderthals lived across much of Eurasia for hundreds of thousands of years before dying out around 40,000 years ago. Denisovans, known mostly from DNA extracted from one remote Siberian cave, lived across much of Asia at roughly the same time. This topic looks at what paleontologists and geneticists have learned about these groups and the ways their DNA still shows up in people today.

tiktaalik.context_blurb: Tiktaalik was a shallow-water fish that lived in what is now Arctic Canada about 375 million years ago. It had fish features, like scales and gills, but also features of a four-limbed land animal, including a mobile neck and limb-like bones in its front fins. Tiktaalik was discovered in 2004 by Neil Shubin's team after a very careful prediction of where fossils of this kind of transitional animal should turn up. It is one of the clearest fossils of the fish-to-tetrapod transition.

whale-evolution-pakicetus-to-modern.context_blurb: Whales descend from four-legged land mammals that walked into shallow water around 50 million years ago. The fossil record now includes a long sequence of transitional forms, from Pakicetus, which still had legs and lived on land, through Ambulocetus and other walking whales, to animals that could no longer walk out of the water at all. This topic looks at the stepping stones in that transition and what each fossil adds to the picture of how a land animal became a whale.

champion-jumpers.context_blurb: Several animals are built almost entirely around jumping. Fleas, grasshoppers, frogs, kangaroo rats, and kangaroos all push off the ground with amounts of force that are extraordinary relative to their body size. This topic looks at the specific anatomical tricks jumping specialists use, from spring-loaded tendons to catapult-style leg muscles, and at the physics that puts a hard ceiling on how far anything with legs can leap.

moving-without-legs.context_blurb: Many animals get around on land without any legs at all. Snakes, worms, slugs, and even certain lizards move by shaping their bodies against the ground in specific ways. This topic looks at the different limbless locomotion styles biologists recognize, from the sidewinding of desert snakes to the muscular waves of earthworms, and at the surprising situations in which no legs can be better than many.

sticking-to-walls.context_blurb: Several animals can climb vertical surfaces and even walk on ceilings. Geckos, tree frogs, flies, and some spiders all stick in different ways. Geckos use microscopic ridges on their toes that take advantage of weak molecular forces; frogs use tiny wet pads; flies use sticky secretions. This topic looks at the different sticking mechanisms and the problems each one has to solve, from falling off to coming unstuck again when the animal wants to move.

the-fastest-runners.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, some animals are built for pure speed on land. Cheetahs, pronghorns, horses, greyhounds, and ostriches all specialize in sprinting or long-distance running. This topic looks at the specific body features that make an animal fast, from leg length and muscle fiber type to spine flexibility, and at the handful of species that come out at the top of each category.

deep-diving-bodies.context_blurb: Several animals, including sperm whales, elephant seals, emperor penguins, and leatherback turtles, dive to depths that would kill any human diver without heavy equipment. The body of a deep diver has to deal with crushing pressure, holding its breath for a very long time, and the problem of how to use oxygen stored in the body rather than in the lungs. This topic looks at the specific body features and chemistry that make a successful deep diver.

jet-propulsion.context_blurb: Several marine animals swim by shooting water out of their bodies in short bursts. Squid, octopuses, jellyfish, scallops, and nautiluses all use jet propulsion to one degree or another. This topic looks at the specific body plumbing each group uses, the trade-offs between fast jetting and slow efficient cruising, and at why jet propulsion keeps turning up in soft-bodied animals that need a sudden burst of speed.

staying-up-or-sinking.context_blurb: Fish and other aquatic animals have to deal with a basic problem: without any help, their bodies are slightly denser than seawater and tend to sink. Different animals have different solutions. Bony fish, sharks, and cephalopods have each landed on a different piece of equipment to solve the problem. This topic looks at the different buoyancy strategies that have evolved in the sea and the trade-offs between them.

the-tuna-body-plan-thunniform-swimming.context_blurb: A specific streamlined body shape, with a crescent-shaped tail, has evolved in several different fast-swimming marine predators, including tunas, mackerels, swordfish, mako sharks, and even some extinct marine reptiles. Biologists call it the thunniform body plan. This topic looks at the hydrodynamics behind sustained high-speed swimming in the open ocean, and at why so many unrelated animals have ended up looking so similar to one another below the waist.

ears-at-the-extremes.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, hearing ranges go far beyond what human ears can pick up. Elephants hear very low frequencies through their feet. Mice and some bats hear ultrasonic frequencies far above us. Owls can locate a mouse under snow by sound alone. This topic looks at the specific ear designs that let animals push the limits of frequency, direction, and sensitivity.

echolocation-built-twice.context_blurb: Several animal groups navigate and hunt by producing sounds and listening for the echoes. Bats, toothed whales, oilbirds, and some cave swiftlets all use echolocation. Biologists have shown that the brain machinery for echolocation evolved separately in bats and whales, which is a textbook case of convergent evolution. This topic looks at how echolocation works and the different animal groups that have re-invented it.

infrasound-and-hearing-through-the-feet.context_blurb: Several large animals, including elephants, giraffes, and some whales, communicate using very low-frequency sounds that travel through air or ground. In elephants, the low frequencies even travel through the ground as vibration, and the animal picks them up through sensitive pads in its feet. This topic looks at the specific low-frequency channels different animals use and the surprising distances that these signals can cover.

the-lateral-line-feeling-the-water-move.context_blurb: Fish and some amphibians have a specialized sense called the lateral line, running down each side of the body. It is tuned to pick up water movement, which lets a fish feel other animals, obstacles, and currents without seeing or hearing them. This topic looks at how the lateral line works, why it is so useful for a schooling fish, and the ways it is being studied as a model for underwater sensing in robots.

endurance-aloft.context_blurb: A number of birds can stay in the air for days, weeks, or even months at a time. Albatrosses, swifts, and frigatebirds all spend most of their lives aloft, sleeping on the wing or barely touching down. This topic looks at the specific flight techniques these endurance fliers use, from dynamic soaring over ocean waves to riding thermals and from how they conserve energy to how they sleep with their brains still steering.

flight-evolved-four-separate-times.context_blurb: True powered flight is rare in nature; biologists usually count four separate times it has evolved: in insects, in pterosaurs, in birds, and in bats. Each case developed from a different starting point and built the wing out of different materials. This topic looks at the four flying lineages, what each one started with, and the specific engineering problems each had to solve to get into the air.

gliding-not-flying.context_blurb: Many animals, including flying squirrels, flying lizards, flying frogs, flying snakes, and flying fish, glide but do not actually fly in the powered sense. Gliding costs much less than flapping flight but is limited to one-way downward journeys. This topic looks at the different gliding membranes and body shapes animals have evolved and at what gliding is good for in forests, oceans, and open country.

hovering-in-place.context_blurb: A handful of animals, hummingbirds, hoverflies, dragonflies, and some hawks, can hold their position in the air without any forward motion. Hovering costs a lot more energy than regular flight and demands very specific wing kinematics. This topic looks at the different hovering techniques animals use, from the figure-eight stroke of a hummingbird to the fast flutter of a hoverfly, and the physics that explains why not every flier can do it.

animals-that-generate-electricity.context_blurb: A few animals produce strong electric shocks of their own. Electric eels of the Amazon, electric catfish of African rivers, and torpedo rays and electric stargazers of the oceans all have specialized muscle tissue that works as a biological battery. This topic looks at the different animals that make their own electricity, what they use the shocks for, and the specific body chemistry behind generating a jolt strong enough to kill prey.

electroreception-reading-the-body-electr.context_blurb: A number of animals, including sharks, rays, platypuses, electric fish, and a handful of amphibians, can detect signals given off by other animals' bodies that most other animals cannot. The sense is called electroreception, and in many species it is detailed enough to pick up a hidden fish's heartbeat. This topic looks at the different animals that can use the sense, the organs that let them do it, and the specific hunting problems the sense solves.

navigating-by-earths-magnetic-field.context_blurb: A number of animals, from pigeons and migratory songbirds to sea turtles, salmon, and even some insects, navigate using Earth's magnetic field. The field varies in predictable ways over the surface of the planet, which gives migrating animals a built-in map. This topic looks at how different animals detect magnetism, where researchers think the receptors sit, and why the physics behind the sense is still an active research mystery.

dunkleosteus.context_blurb: Dunkleosteus was a huge armored fish that lived in the oceans about 360 million years ago, late in the Devonian period. It is one of the most famous of the placoderms, an extinct group of fish with heavy bony armor on their heads and shoulders.
