Dunkleosteus had no actual teeth; instead, the edges of its jaw bones were sharpened into slicing plates that opened and closed with astonishing force. It was the top predator of its time.

helicoprion.context_blurb: Helicoprion was a strange, shark-like fish that lived in the oceans about 290 million years ago. For over a century, paleontologists knew it only from a single fossil: a spiral whorl of about 150 interlocking teeth. Nobody could agree on where in the body the spiral went. Modern CT-scan work on the best Idaho specimens finally placed the whorl inside the lower jaw, and the animal's anatomy is slowly coming into focus.

megalodon.context_blurb: Megalodon was a huge shark that lived in oceans around the world from about 23 to 3.6 million years ago. It is almost certainly the largest shark that ever lived, with teeth more than seven inches long. Megalodon is known mostly from its teeth, which are abundant in Miocene and Pliocene sediments, and from a handful of vertebrae. This topic looks at what paleontologists have figured out about its size, ecology, and why it went extinct, as well as what pop culture tends to get wrong about it.

ichthyosaur.context_blurb: The ichthyosaurs were a group of large marine reptiles that lived in the oceans for most of the Mesozoic, from about 250 to 90 million years ago. They were shaped like dolphins or tuna, with streamlined bodies and vertical tail flukes, but they were reptiles, not fish or mammals. Ichthyosaurs are a textbook case of convergent evolution, and the first scientifically described one was found by Mary Anning on the English coast in the early 1800s.

mosasaur.context_blurb: Mosasaurs were a group of huge marine reptiles that lived in the oceans from about 100 million to 66 million years ago, dying out at the same mass extinction that killed the non-bird dinosaurs. They were long, snake-headed, flipper-driven predators, with jaws built like a snake's for swallowing large prey. This topic looks at where mosasaurs fit in the reptile family tree, how big they got, and what has been learned from well-preserved skeletons in Kansas, the Netherlands, and Morocco.

plesiosaur.context_blurb: The plesiosaurs were a group of large marine reptiles that lived in the oceans for most of the Mesozoic. They had two body shapes: a short-necked, big-headed form sometimes called the pliosaurs, and a long-necked, small-headed form that gave the whole group its popular image. The long-necked plesiosaur body is often the inspiration behind sea-monster illustrations, from the Loch Ness monster to many cartoons. This topic looks at how plesiosaurs actually lived and swam.

scent-trails-and-the-moth-that-smells-a-.context_blurb: Many animals, from ants to moths to mammals, communicate with chemical trails and plumes. A male silk moth can detect the scent of a female from several kilometers away using a tiny number of specialized receptors on his huge feathered antennae. Ants lay down pheromone trails to lead nestmates to food. This topic looks at the chemistry of scent communication, the specific sensory organs animals use to pick up these cues, and the surprising distances a scent can carry a message across still air.

super-smellers.context_blurb: Some animals have senses of smell much more powerful than ours. Bloodhounds, bears, elephants, moths, and sharks are all famous for exceptional olfaction. The record-holder, by some measures, is the African elephant. This topic looks at how a sense of smell is measured, which animals come out on top, and what an exceptional sense of smell actually buys an animal in the wild.

tasting-with-the-whole-body.context_blurb: Several animals have taste receptors on parts of their bodies that no vertebrate textbook would call obvious. Catfish taste with much of their outer surface; octopus arms taste with their suckers; butterflies taste with their feet. This topic looks at the animals that have moved chemical sensing out of the mouth, what each one uses that distributed taste for, and the different ways the sensory tissue is wired.

feeling-in-the-dark-the-touch-specialist.context_blurb: A number of animals navigate and hunt mostly by touch. Certain moles, catfish, and naked mole-rats all live in environments where sight is almost useless and rely on specialized touch organs instead. This topic looks at how touch-specialist animals solve the problem of mapping the world without seeing it, and at the surprising speeds some of them can process a tactile scene.

seeing-heat-the-pit-vipers-infrared-eye.context_blurb: A handful of snakes, including pit vipers and some boas and pythons, can see the heat given off by warm-blooded prey. They do it with specialized pit organs on the sides of their faces, which work like infrared cameras. This topic looks at the way these pit organs feed their signals into the snake's brain, how the two sides combine to give the snake something close to a thermal image of its surroundings, and the limits of this sense.

pterosaur-quetzalcoatlus.context_blurb: Quetzalcoatlus was a huge pterosaur that lived in what is now Texas at the end of the age of the dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. Pterosaurs are an extinct group of winged animals that were close cousins of the dinosaurs rather than true dinosaurs themselves. Quetzalcoatlus was one of the largest animals that has ever taken to the air. Modern paleontology has had to carefully work out how such a huge animal could have taken off at all, and what it was doing on the ground when it was not aloft.
